articles.content_orig:
The chief executive of Dr. Martens has been named the Black British Business Person of the Year at the 2026 Black British Business Awards (BBBAwards).
Ije Nwokorie, who became chief of Dr. Martens in January last year and is the only black chief executive in the FTSE 250, was awarded in recognition of his role shaping Dr. Martens’ growth strategy.
He is recognised inside Dr. Martens for his strong communication with staff, according to the judges.
Before joining Dr. Martens, Mr Nwokorie spent more than 11 years at Wolff Olins, the marketing giant, before working as a senior director at Apple.
Born in the US but brought up from age six against the backdrop of post-civil-war Nigeria, Mr Nwokorie has described how he and his family went from the lifestyle trappings of 1960s America to a small Nigerian village and a home with no running water.
On winning the award, Mr Nwokorie said: “This recognition means a lot to me. While this award bears my name, it reflects the talent, dedication and generosity of the incredible teammates, mentors and leaders who have shaped me as a person and a professional.
“It is a powerful reminder that there is nothing more important in our leadership journeys than the time we invest to help others thrive.”
Alongside his executive career, he has served as a trustee at Charity: water for nearly a decade and held board roles at cultural and humanitarian organisations including the Institute of International Visual Arts and Malaria No More UK.
He also served as chairman of trustees for the Chineke! Orchestra, a British orchestra championing change and the first in Europe to feature a majority of black and ethnically diverse musicians.
The Black British Business Awards started in 2014 to celebrate the achievements of black people in British business. The Telegraph is the national media partner for the awards.
Mr Nwokorie was presented with the award at an exclusive ceremony sponsored by JPMorgan Chase at London’s Hilton Park Lane hotel.
Speaking at the ceremony, Sophie Chandauka, the executive founder of the awards, said: “You lend the BBBAwards credibility not simply to celebrate excellence, but to ensure the best and brightest from all communities get a fair shot. That commitment has made the BBBAwards the UK’s premium awards programme for black business achievement.”
A spokesman for JPMorgan Chase said: “We couldn’t be prouder to support and celebrate such an outstanding breadth of black British talent.
“Their accomplishments continue to inspire future generations and demonstrate the exceptional value they bring to businesses, communities and the wider UK economy.”
This year’s winners are as follows:
Black British Business Person of the Year : Ije Nwokorie, chief executive of Dr Martens
Arts and Media Rising Star : Sheniece Charway, artist partnership manager [EMEA], YouTube/Google
Arts and Media Senior Leader : Amie Parker-Williams, director, digital commissioning and production, Paramount
Fashion, Beauty and Consumer Senior Leader : Andrea Thompson, journalist, brand consultant and former editor-in-chief, Marie Claire UK
Fashion, Beauty and Consumer Rising Star : Yasmin O’Neal, senior director for global brand and impact, DECIEM
Entrepreneur Rising Star : Dr Elsa Zekeng, founder and chief executive, SökerData
Entrepreneur Senior Leader : Antonia Okonma Shittu, founder and chief executive, A-List Lace Hair
Financial Services Rising Star : Nana Agyemang, proposition delivery manager, Barclays
Financial Services Senior Leader : Melissa Max-Macarthy, formerly managing director, head of strategy and innovation, retail banking, NatWest Group
Professional Services Rising Star : Jack Van Cooten, senior manager – external vendors and data, Oliver Wyman
Professional Services Senior Leader : Laurie-Anne Power KC, barrister, 25 Bedford Row
Retail and Hospitality Senior Leader : Leona De Graft, vice-president of global ecommerce, Levi Strauss and Co
Retail and Hospitality Rising Star : Rickey Devonish, head of apprenticeships and emerging talent, JD Group

articles.title_orig: Tesla’s China business is flipping: sales down 12%, exports double
articles.title_zh: Tesla’s China business is flipping: sales down 12%, exports double
articles.content_orig:
Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers through the first nine months of 2026, down 11.9% from last year, according to CPCA data. Over the same period, Giga Shanghai’s exports more than doubled to 361,972 vehicles.
Nearly half of what Tesla builds in China now leaves China. And Beijing just announced it will cut the tax rebate on EV exports next year.
When Tesla broke ground on Giga Shanghai in January 2019 , Elon Musk was clear about who the factory was for.
“Shanghai Giga will produce affordable versions of 3/Y for greater China,” Musk wrote at the time. He added that the Model S, Model X and “higher cost versions” of the Model 3 and Model Y would “still be built in US for WW market, incl China.” In another post that same week, he summed up the philosophy: “Affordable cars must be made on same continent as customers.”
That lasted about a year and a half. By late 2020, Shanghai was building right-hand-drive Model 3s for Australia and New Zealand and shipping Model 3s to Europe. Today it supplies Europe, Asia-Pacific and, since this year, Canada again under Ottawa’s new China EV import quota .
None of those customers are on the same continent as Shanghai.
Here’s how Tesla’s China business looks through September, based on CPCA data:
The domestic number is the lowest first nine months Tesla has posted in China in at least four years. It’s down 17% from the 460,203 cars Tesla sold there over the same period in 2024.
Q3 was worse. Tesla’s Chinese retail sales fell 16% to 142,133 units, and July alone was down 33%. September (64,837 units, down 9.4%) was the best month of the quarter, but it was still a decline.
The whole Chinese EV market is shrinking this year, so some of this isn’t Tesla-specific. NEV retail sales in China are down 12.8% through September, according to the CPCA, after Beijing cut the purchase tax exemption in half on January 1. So Tesla is roughly tracking the market year-to-date. But in Q3, the market was down about 10% and Tesla was down 16%.
You wouldn’t know any of this from Tesla China’s headline numbers. Wholesale, which counts both domestic sales and exports, is up 22.5% this year, and July’s 93,579 units was the factory’s best July ever.
That’s all exports. Tesla has already shipped more cars out of China this year (361,972) than it did in all of 2023 (344,078), 2024 (259,548) or 2025 (226,034).
As we pointed out in our H1 analysis , Shanghai has become Tesla’s pressure valve. It can keep running near capacity even as Chinese buyers walk away, because the cars go somewhere else.
And it’s carrying the whole company. Shanghai’s wholesale volume in Q3 was 275,111 vehicles, equal to 57% of the 486,532 cars Tesla delivered worldwide . Chinese buyers accounted for just 29%.
On Monday, China’s Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration announced that the VAT export rebate on new energy vehicles will drop from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027. It covers battery-electric and plug-in hybrid cars, and the rate is based on the export date on the customs declaration.
It’s part of a pattern. Beijing already eliminated the export rebate on solar panels in April, and the battery rebate was cut from 9% to 6% and goes to zero on January 1, 2027.
The mechanics are simple. Chinese exporters get the VAT they paid refunded when a product leaves the country. Whatever isn’t refunded becomes a cost. So starting in April, automakers eat an extra 4% of the export value on every EV they ship out of China.
For Tesla, that’s real money. Assuming an average export value of around ¥220,000 per Model 3 or Model Y, the cut costs about ¥8,800 ($1,235) per car. At this year’s export pace of roughly 480,000 vehicles a year, that’s around $600 million annually that Tesla either absorbs or passes on to buyers in Europe, Canada and Asia. That’s our estimate, not a Tesla figure.
Tesla isn’t alone. China exported more than 4 million NEVs in the first nine months of the year, more than double last year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Every Chinese automaker that’s been using exports to offset weak demand at home gets the same bill.
But few are as exposed as Tesla, with half its Chinese production going abroad and its domestic sales falling.
There’s one more effect to watch. Since the rate depends on the customs declaration date, expect automakers, Tesla included, to cram as many exports as possible into Q4 and Q1 before the deadline. That should make Tesla China’s wholesale numbers look great for two more quarters, before the cost shows up in Q2 2027.
Musk said Giga Shanghai would build affordable cars for China. It did, for about a year. Then it became Tesla’s export hub, and now it’s more than that: it’s the thing propping up Tesla’s China numbers and a big chunk of its global deliveries.
That shift was a reaction to falling demand. Tesla’s lineup in China is still the Model 3 and Model Y, while BYD, Xiaomi, Xpeng and a dozen others launch new models every few months at lower prices. Chinese buyers have options, and fewer of them are picking Tesla. Exports let Tesla keep the factory busy without cutting production, and the “record” wholesale did the rest.
Beijing’s rebate cut makes that model more expensive. Tesla has three options, and none of them are good. It can raise prices abroad, in markets like Europe where its sales are already weak. It can eat a margin hit of roughly $600 million a year at a time when its automotive margins are already thin. Or it can build fewer cars in Shanghai.
Berlin could take on more Model Y volume for Europe, but that doesn’t help the Model 3, Canada or Asia-Pacific.
So the question for 2027 is this: what happens to Giga Shanghai when both its home market and its export valve shrink at the same time?

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘rapid’ decline as nearly 63% of population lost to starvation
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘rapid’ decline as nearly 63% of population lost to starvation
articles.content_orig:
The (former) world’s largest penguin colony on Zavodovski Island has lost its long-held title following a dramatic population collapse.
Research by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) shows chinstrap penguins on the remote volcanic island suffered a severe decline from around 1.09 million breeding individuals in January 2011 to just 402,000 in 2025 — a drop of nearly two-thirds occurring at a sharp 7% annual rate. Lead study author Norman Ratcliffe described the decline as “very rapid.”
Because of this steep drop, Zavodovski Island has lost its distinction as Earth’s largest penguin colony – a title that now belongs to the Adélie penguin colony at Cape Adare on the opposite side of Antarctica , which was estimated to number over one million birds as of 2018.
BAS researchers attribute the collapse to human-driven climate change, noting that climate-driven changes near Antarctica have upended ocean food chains.
Winter temperatures around the Antarctic Peninsula have surged by 5°C above pre-industrial levels, marking one of the fastest warming rates on Earth. “We think that climate change operating through food webs is probably the main driver,” Ratcliffe said about the population decline in the study.
Rising ocean temperatures have pushed Antarctic krill — the tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that serve as the chinstraps’ primary food source — further south into colder waters that chinstraps do not tolerate. As a result, the birds face a life-threatening dilemma: follow their food into unsuitable habitats or remain and risk starvation.
Because chinstrap and macaroni penguins – Zavodovski’s other inhabitants – thrive in different temperature ranges, warming waters affect them differently.
Zavodovski grew from roughly 338,000 in 2011 to 433,000 in 2025, now outnumbering the chinstraps. Together, the two species still total more than 835,000 birds on the island.
Summarizing these ecological changes, the BAS study concluded: “The most plausible explanation for the observed patterns of population change is that a climate-induced regime shift has occurred that has been detrimental to the maritime Antarctic chinstraps but has favored the subantarctic macaronis.”
To measure the full scale of the decline, BAS researchers sailed 15 days to reach the remote island and deployed drones over the colony. In a video released on social media, the BAS detailed how chinstraps may now qualify as an endangered species.
Zavodovski Island, dominated by Mount Curry and its volcanic ash plains, is typically blanketed by penguins, with the South Sandwich Islands hosting 38% of the global chinstrap population. However, rising ocean temperatures continue to pose a grave threat to their long-term survival.
Researchers ruled out local volcanic eruptions as the cause of the decline. Despite initial fears when Mount Curry erupted in 2016, satellite images and field measurements showed that the main ash cloud blew northeast, away from the core nesting grounds. The prevailing macaroni penguin species was further proof that the eruption was not the downfall of chinstraps.
“The decline in chinstrap colony area was in progress prior to the eruption and continued at a constant rate thereafter,” the BAS study noted. Ratcliffe added, “We don’t think the volcano is implicated or it’s not the main driver because what we see is a linear decline in the chinstrap penguins.”

articles.title_orig: One dead, several others hurt on Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia
articles.title_zh: One dead, several others hurt on Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This article contains some graphic details
One person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.
The Cobb County Police Department is investigating the fatality at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, a local official confirmed.
The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.
Horrified witnesses have told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride - something the BBC has not verified.
Six Flags said it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.
It said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".
Lisa Cupid, the chairwoman of Cobb County's governing body, said police detectives with the local major crimes unit "are investigating the circumstances surrounding this incident".
The man who died has been identified as Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, who lived in nearby Atlanta, the Cobb County Police Department told the BBC.
Details about how he died and how other riders were injured have not yet been released but the BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials.
Local outlet 11 Alive quoted a witness saying Kariem had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction.
The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added.
A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told 11 Alive that Kariem fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off.
"We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a girl covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believes she saw the man ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," Landry said.
A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately and that they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident.
Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.
The death in Georgia comes just weeks after one of Six Flags' parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.
Six Flags said that ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire the attraction because it was "the right thing to do".

articles.title_orig: UConn Law Students Gain Real-World Experience in Criminal Defense Victory
articles.title_zh: UConn Law Students Gain Real-World Experience in Criminal Defense Victory
articles.content_orig:
October 13, 2026 | Meagan Fazio
Working alongside Connecticut public defenders, students in the Criminal Defense Appellate Clinic helped secure a new trial in a murder case while developing skills in appellate advocacy and community service.
Catherine Cheek ’26 stood before the Connecticut Supreme Court to argue a murder appeal. (CT-N)
The week after completing her final exams at UConn School of Law last spring, Catherine Cheek ’26 stood before the Connecticut Supreme Court to argue a murder appeal.
She and fellow clinic student Justin Taverna ’26 were working on State v. Sellers through UConn Law’s Criminal Defense Appellate Clinic . Offered in partnership with the Connecticut Division of Public Defender Services, the clinic allows students to work on criminal appeals under the supervision of experienced appellate attorneys.
Under the guidance of Connecticut public defenders and UConn Law adjunct professors Erica Barber ’14 and Jennifer Bourn ’04, both former clinic students, Cheek and Taverna helped develop the appeal. Cheek remained with the clinic for an additional year to prepare a reply brief and present part of the oral argument. Their efforts contributed to a significant victory when, on August 25, the Connecticut Supreme Court reversed Rashad Tee Sellers’ murder conviction and ordered a new trial.
The case illustrates how the clinic combines legal training, mentorship, and public service.
“The Criminal Defense Appellate Clinic demonstrates the benefits of clinical legal education,” says Jessica Rubin , associate dean for experiential education. “Students learn by handling complex matters under expert supervision, while helping to provide legal representation to clients and serving communities across Connecticut.”
Sellers had been convicted of murder and sentenced to serve 50 years in prison. The appeal centered on scientific evidence that the state used to connect him to the crime, including lead particles found on his clothing that were described as being associated with gunshot residue.
Over the course of the appeal, the students reviewed the trial court’s record, researched the relevant scientific and legal issues, and helped develop the defense’s arguments. Cheek ultimately presented the opening portion of the oral argument before the Connecticut Supreme Court, just days after completing her final exams.
Although arguing before the state’s highest court was initially intimidating, Cheek says extensive preparation helped calm any nerves.
“Erica coordinated about five different practice moots with a variety of students and practitioners to make sure I was fully ready,” Cheek explains. “Their feedback was immensely helpful, and I was able to improve my argument with each round. When the big day arrived, I was a little nervous, but I felt confident in my knowledge and ready to discuss the case with the court.”
The Supreme Court ruled that the trial court should have more carefully evaluated the reliability of the evidence before admitting it. Because that review never occurred, the court overturned the conviction and ordered a new trial. The court also noted that the gunshot residue evidence was the only link between Sellers and the firearm used in the homicide.
Learning While Serving Clients
The Criminal Defense Appellate Clinic typically enrolls five or six students and handles about three cases each year, including murder appeals, Fourth Amendment issues, search-and-seizure questions, and motor vehicle stop cases. Since its launch, four clinic cases have reached final disposition, with victories in three, including two murder appeals.
The depth of the students’ involvement benefits both their education and the clinic’s representation of clients. For Cheek, the significance of that responsibility became especially clear after meeting the client.
“I remember the weight and importance of the appeal hitting me after I met the client and wondering whether I was equipped to take on a case like this,” Cheek said. “Luckily, I had two incredible attorneys as mentors, so over time the weight of the case stopped being something that caused me to hesitate or doubt myself and started being something that motivated me to push myself.”
That combination of responsibility and close faculty mentorship is a defining feature of the clinic. Students spend substantial time studying their cases, developing knowledge that can strengthen the clinic’s representation of clients.
“We spend so much class time and have so many additional brains and really bright people who are reviewing the case materials and bringing their ideas and thinking them through,” Bourn says.
Students also bring fresh perspectives that can challenge assumptions experienced attorneys may take for granted.
“I think the students see the injustice that maybe we’ve become not blind to, but used to,” Barber says.
For Barber and Bourn, teaching the clinic continues a tradition that helped shape their own careers. Both participated in UConn Law’s appellate and trial clinics as students during what Bourn called the “Tim Everett and Todd Fernow era.”
“My whole career is attributable to the clinic,” Barber says.
She credits the clinic with leading to her first judicial clerkship and first law firm job. That mentorship continues today. Fernow still returns as a guest lecturer, and Barber regularly seeks his advice on challenging legal issues.
Bourn says the clinic confirmed her decision to pursue public defense work.
“The clinic was really the first time in law school that I felt like, ‘Oh yeah, this is why I came. This is what I want to be doing.’”
Today, Barber and Bourn hope to provide the same support for their own students, encouraging graduates to stay connected as they build careers in criminal defense, appellate advocacy, and public service.

articles.title_orig: Inside Robert’s Western World: Nashville’s classic honky tonk
articles.title_zh: Inside Robert’s Western World: Nashville’s classic honky tonk
articles.content_orig:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( Aging Untold ) — Lower Broadway is known for high-rise honky tonks and rooftop bars that draw crowds late into the night. Under a large red boot sign sits Robert’s Western World, a bar that plays only traditional country music.
Robert’s Western World has operated for more than 30 years. The bar sells cans of beer starting at $2.50.
“We’ve left it alone. It’s not broke. Don’t fix it,” owner Emily Jones said.
Jones and her husband, JesseLee, own Robert’s Western World and are working to keep its legacy going.
“A time capsule when people walk in here,” Emily Jones said. “We are in a society where people are longing for something tangible. They want to know the history.”
JesseLee Jones moved to Nashville from Brazil and worked at Robert’s Western World before getting the chance to buy it.
“Do what’s in your heart, because if you do what’s in your heart, you don’t work a day in your life,” he said.
JesseLee Jones said the bar does not have a television inside.
“You come in here and it’s like stepping back into the 50s, and the 60s, and the 70s, the heydays of country music,” he said.
The walls are covered with photos of some of country music’s biggest names, who have been regulars at the bar, including Dolly Parton and Waylon Jennings.
“They just want to tuck in the crowd, have a beer and just be human and take in the vibe,” Emily Jones said.
The bar was named one of USA Today’s best bars in the country.
Emily and JesseLee Jones have bought the building next door and plan to expand Robert’s Western World.
“But it will still be Nashville. It will still be real,” JesseLee Jones said. “And that is what’s missing nowadays. Believability.”

articles.title_orig: 28 Miles and Counting: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Sets a Mars Driving Record
articles.title_zh: 28 Miles and Counting: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Sets a Mars Driving Record
articles.content_orig:
This animated orbital-map view shows the route NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has taken from time of its 2021 landing to Oct. 11, 2026 — the day it broke the off-world driving record previously held by the agency’s Opportunity rover. As of that date, Perseverance has driven over 28 miles (45 kilometers).
The six-wheeled geologist has in less than six years surpassed a mark set by the agency’s Opportunity rover, which explored the Red Planet for nearly 15 years.
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has driven farther than any vehicle ever has on the surface of another world. On Oct. 11, the rover’s odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), eclipsing the record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which explored Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance reached the mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.
The milestone came as Perseverance traveled toward an area called “Idubi” through the region off the western rim of Jezero Crater nicknamed “Lac de Charmes,” where the rover is investigating what may be some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system. The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates), and Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems.
Much of the credit belongs to Perseverance’s self-driving capability. Using an autonomous navigation system known as AutoNav , the rover images the terrain while rolling, builds a 3D map of hazards, and plots its course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth — a capability the team calls “thinking while driving.” Perseverance can do all that at or near its top speed , covering as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single sol. The six-wheeled scientist has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain, compared with about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. Where NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner , assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points, Perseverance processes 600,000 with every look.
One of Perseverance’s navigation cameras captured this shot on Oct. 11, 2026, the Martian day, or sol, that a 299.6-foot (91.31-meter) drive pushed the rover’s total mileage past Opportunity’s 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record on Mars.
“It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,” said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.”
NASA recently approved the mission’s first extension, which began in October and will carry Perseverance’s exploration of the crater rim through roughly the end of 2028.
Perseverance’s record caps nearly three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars, each mission driving farther and more capably than the last.
The microwave-oven-size Sojourner rover covered about 330 feet (100 meters) during its 83-sol mission in 1997. The golf-cart-size twins Spirit and Opportunity arrived in 2004 with 90-sol prime missions. Spirit logged 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) before succumbing to the Martian winter in 2010. Opportunity kept rolling for 5,111 sols, completing the first extraterrestrial marathon in 2015 and setting the record Perseverance has now surpassed. The agency’s Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and remains hard at work, has logged more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers).
“The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,” Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance. “Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive. The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the Sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.”
This infographic illustrates the distances driven by various rovers on the surface of Earth’s Moon and Mars. Of the vehicles shown, the NASA Mars rovers Perseverance and Curiosity are still operational and moving across the surface; the figures shown for those two are distances driven as of Oct. 11, 2026.
The extraterrestrial off-road driving record isn’t limited to Mars: Lunar driving records were broken earlier in the journey. Perseverance rolled past both the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972 and the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) driven by the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.
Setting distance records is just a bonus. Stamina and longer drives are putting more geologic diversity within reach faster — more outcrops examined and more of the Red Planet’s history read from its rocks. That reach carried Perseverance from an ancient lakebed up a fossilized river system, where the rover found a potential biosignature at a rock called “Cheyava Falls,” and on to the crater rim, where an entirely different kind of ancient habitat — hydrothermal — may await.
Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples spanning the crater floor, a delta fan formed by a long-gone river, and now the crater rim. In the latter region, it has been exploring impact-generated rocks some 4 billion years old, from a chapter of planetary history almost entirely erased on Earth.
After Lac de Charmes, the rover will continue along the crater rim and head south during the extended mission towards Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide (100-meter-wide) block of ancient crust uplifted by the impact that created Jezero.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.

articles.title_orig: White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign amid misconduct allegations
articles.title_zh: White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign amid misconduct allegations
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, resigns amid misconduct allegations
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle , once a top campaign surrogate for President Donald Trump, has resigned amid a misconduct probe.
“Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime,” Guilfoyle said Tuesday in a post on X announcing her resignation.
She also addressed “recent allegations against me, writing that “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
Guilfoyle’s post came shortly after new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters that Guilfoyle had been asked to step down.
“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” Zacharia said at her inaugural White House press briefing. “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
Speaking to reporters later Tuesday morning, Trump said of Guilfoyle that “She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading.”
He added that he had not spoken to her.
Guilfoyle, 57, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., has been under investigation by the State Department’s inspector general’s office, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News last week.
The probe came after The Wall Street Journal reported allegations of misconduct in her role as ambassador, including allegations that she bragged about her connections to Greek tycoons who she said funded luxury trips for her. The article cited people who heard the conversation and an audio recording. NBC News has not independently confirmed the allegations.
A Trump donor named Eric Deters came forward this month accusing her of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 Senate confirmation hearing in exchange for access to senior administration officials.
“She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview.
“She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he added.
A text message provided by Deters appeared to show Guilfoyle instructing him to wire the money directly to American Express because “it won’t show up anywhere” that way. He said he did not pay her the money.
Attorneys for Guilfoyle said in a statement Monday that Deters owed her the money for speaking engagements, which he denies.
The attorneys, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also denied allegations of any impropriety involving her travel, saying she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”
Asked Tuesday whether she was would launch her own investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, referred back to the State Department probe.
“I think right now that there is an inspector general investigation in the Department of State. We’ll probably wait to see what comes, what happens with that,” Pirro told reporters.
After the reports about her misconduct first surfaced last week, Guilfoyle thought she could save her job and was making calls to allies as recently as yesterday in a continued effort to do that, according to a source familiar with the matter.
The person added that there was concern among senior White House aides about what a State Department inspector general probe would find and reveal that has not been made public yet and that could be embarrassing for the president and his administration.
Asked Friday about the reports of Guilfoyle’s conduct, Trump said it was “too bad.”
“I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice,” he said.
His tone had hardened by Monday. Asked whether he was considering firing her, he said: “We’re looking at it. We’re not happy.”
Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Guilfoyle last week.
Vance said “these are accusations” and “we don’t try people in the court of public opinion.”
“Let’s actually see what the facts are. Let’s see what the truth is, and obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said.
Rubio, meanwhile, ripped a reporter for asking about the allegations while he was with her in Athens.
“We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you,” Rubio said Thursday.
“I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: World Food Day 2026: Global Hunger Has Declined, but Gains Are Fragile
articles.title_zh: World Food Day 2026: Global Hunger Has Declined, but Gains Are Fragile
articles.content_orig:
In 2015, the United Nations adopted the Sustainable Development Goals , a global commitment to end poverty, protect the planet and promote peace and prosperity for all people by 2030.
As World Food Day approaches on October 16, the United Nation’s 2026 State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) report offers a snapshot of progress and ongoing challenges in the fight against hunger. While hunger declined in some regions in 2025, climate change, food inflation and conflict threaten this progress, particularly in Africa. Th e UN estimates that 7.8 percent of the world’s population is facing hunger, and for the first time, Africa now hosts the largest number of people in the world who do not get enough to eat .
CWS reaffirms the urgent need to address the root causes of hunger and ensure everyone has access to the safe, adequate, affordable, nutritious food they need to thrive.
“Having enough to feed my children means regaining my dignity and my place in life.”
— Victorine , CWS Food Security and Livelihoods Program Participant
The ability to access adequate food and nutrition to meet daily needs is a basic human right. Yet more than 645 million people around the world faced hunger last year.
The world produces enough food to feed everyone. Hunger persists not because of scarcity, but because of systemic barriers such as poverty, inequality, conflict and climate-related disasters.
Drawing on findings from the 2026 SOFI report , several interconnected factors continue to drive hunger and food insecurity around the world:
While the number of people in the world going to bed hungry every night has declined since 2022, the numbers are still higher than they were before the COVID-19 pandemic, and hunger has gotten worse in some regions.
Food security means more than having enough calories to eat. It means having consistent access to safe, nutritious and diverse foods that support health and well-being.
Healthy diets help children learn and grow, prevents disease and supports healthy aging and boosts productivity. Yet healthy foods are unaffordable for roughly one in three people around the world.
CWS works alongside communities to address the root causes of hunger and poverty through locally led food security programs. From climate-smart agriculture to sustainable livelihoods and economic opportunities to advocacy and training for small-scale farmers, we partner with families to build pathways out of hunger.
In Cambodia , CWS is empowering farmers to increase crop production, earn more income and adapt to changing weather patterns and growing conditions through climate-smart agriculture and Farmer Field Schools.
In Tanzania , CWS partners with refugees living in Nyarugusu Refugee Camp to ensure they have enough nutritious food when food stocks are low between harvests, while helping them pursue resilient livelihoods.
In Nicaragua , CWS provides resources and training that help families grow food, build savings and withstand droughts and other climate threats.
For 80 years, CWS has partnered with communities around the world to ensure everyone has access to the resources they need to thrive. Together, we can build a world where there is enough for all.

articles.title_orig: Employees all over the world find themselves monitored by AI at work
articles.title_zh: Employees all over the world find themselves monitored by AI at work
articles.content_orig:
The latest example of workers under surveillance comes from Co-op, a British consumer co-operative that runs thousands of businesses
This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here .
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while moving laundry from the washer to the dryer, wishing a robot could do the task for me. Today in tech, we’re talking about workers and AI.
Employees across the globe are increasingly finding themselves minutely monitored in their workplaces, with tiny changes in their behaviors resulting in negative performance evaluations.
The latest example of workers under surveillance and bristling at it comes from Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies in the UK. The company implemented an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers.
In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyze and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates.
“You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity.
Read more: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance
The Co-op said it did not recognize the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged.
Resentment of workers’ treatment is already translating into policy, a break from the sluggishness of most technology regulations. Across the Atlantic and the continental United States, California governor Gavin Newsom signed laws into effect last week that prohibit certain types of workplace surveillance.
California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, a California hospital chain, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions.
Read more: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs
*** Tell us: Are you being watched at work?
Tell us: have you been monitored or assessed by AI at work?
Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire
The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
Two stories recently published in the Guardian’s Reworked series pose the question: who is AI enriching?
The first story details how the AI boom is leaving women out of the single largest engine of growth in the US economy. One visible example: Donald Trump’s all-male summit of AI leaders last week: not a single woman in sight as the president preached the power of “superintelligence” .
“We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”
Read more: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
after newsletter promotion
Across AI-related occupations, the median pay of men is $45,000 higher than that of women, partly due to the types of jobs men and women are more likely to have, according to research by LinkedIn: men are still typically hired for higher-paying roles in the AI industry.
When pitching investors, one female co-founder of an AI startup said she has found through trial and error that she and her male co-founder are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.
Another story in the series examines how dire working conditions can become under the pressures of AI and automation. Refugees in Kenya are completing tasks for foreign technology companies under bizarre and opaque conditions.
The stories of desperate remote data workers used to highlight the low pay and horrid content they were exposed to. Today, workers who spoke to the Guardian say they aren’t even sure they will be paid, as their compensation is tied to a so-called “reward” system that decides whether they receive payment based on the quality of their work. Many of the workers called the system unfair but also said with dismay that they had few, if any, other options.
Read more: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
The workers in Kenya also expressed a desperation to earn any money at these jobs before AI could carry out the rote tasks they were assigned.
Contrast these stories of unequal benefit with Sam Altman’s recent remarks on a podcast: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”
Altman was referring to the consequences of AI like the hack of Hugging Face or the attempted creation of bioweapons by would-be terrorists. Bad, to be sure, but lacking the moral outrage of human consequences.

articles.title_orig: Solo show ‘Baggage Claim’ to make world premiere at Cook Theatre
articles.title_zh: Solo show ‘Baggage Claim’ to make world premiere at Cook Theatre
articles.content_orig:
SARASOTA, Fla. (WWSB) - Lifeline Productions is presenting the world premiere of “Baggage Claim,” a solo show performed by actress Danielle Jacobs and directed by Meg Gilbert.
Lifeline Productions describes itself as a theatrical production company focused on using theater to promote mental health and to foster empathy, connection and healing through entertainment.
The show is set in an airport terminal and uses travel mishaps, including delays, missed connections, lost-and-found and final boarding, as a backdrop. According to Lifeline Productions, the production asks what happens when people are forced to confront what they have been running from.
The play is based on Jacobs’ life. Lifeline Productions describes the show as a reckoning with trauma, stigma and the process of healing, and says it addresses the silence surrounding mental health.
“Baggage Claim” runs October 9-18 at the Jane B. Cook Theatre, located at 5555 N Tamiami Trail in Sarasota, inside the FSU Center for the Performing Arts.
Evening performances are scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Weekend matinees are scheduled for 2 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Inside the World of Degenerates , Off-Broadway's Hot New Play About Incels
articles.title_zh: Inside the World of Degenerates , Off-Broadway's Hot New Play About Incels
articles.content_orig:
Playwright Else Went, director Emma Rosa Went, and stars Zachary Desmond and Christopher Dylan White discuss the search for connection in this Playwrights Horizons production.
The off-Broadway play on everybody’s lips this fall is Else Went’s Degenerates , a provocative peek inside the online world of the American incel community. The Playwrights Horizons production, directed by Went’s longtime collaborator and spouse Emma Rosa Went, received the kind of rapturous reviews that any artist would dream of, and tickets for the remainder of the run, through November 1, are scarce.
Degenerates , which begins with a call to a suicide hotline and ends, nearly three hours later, in both hopeful and horrific ways, is one of the first works, if not the first work, to really examine the fallout from the pandemic on a whole generation of isolated young men who believe their bodies make them unlovable. That’s certainly the case for the play’s dual-protagonists, 28-year-old virgin Miller (Zachary Desmond), who runs an incel Discord server, and Target (Christopher Dylan White), a 21-year-old agoraphobic dropout who makes money by doing niche online sex work.
Can Target and Miller actually find camaraderie? That’s the question the Wents have on their mind, one that Desmond and White have been figuring out an answer to since they got an early version of the script four years ago. Together, they’re all trying to figure out whether lonely people can find connection in a world that seems determined to keep them apart.
This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Else, what made you interested in writing about the subject of incels to begin with? Else Went : There are a lot of intersecting reasons. One of them is that there are kids across America killing themselves every day. Another is that a lot of those people find themselves in communities online, which do not seek to better them, but seek to confirm and exacerbate their sense of isolation. There’s an overlap, I think, between people who are exploring trans identity and people who feel like failed men, which is something that incels often say about themselves, and also that repressing trans women say about themselves.
It became an exploration into the language of these spaces and the psychology of what is permitted to be said and how that creates this ideology of disenfranchisement that digs people deeper into a hole where everybody’s got a shovel and nobody’s trying to climb out.
And then seeing what it would be like to explore a version where people from these groups find a way out.
Without giving away too much, it does feel to me that it’s almost like a romcom for certain characters, and then a grand tragedy for others. Like, it’s sweet and horrific at the same time. Emma Rosa Went : I’m glad that you experienced it as a tragedy. I’m glad you also exited feeling hopeful. The tension between those two points is what we’re interested in. The tentative tendrils of happiness and health that [certain characters] are moving toward are held in balance with Miller’s endpoint, which is not only politically chilling but is also a very American kind of queer tragedy. It’s not the kind of tragedy that we’re conditioned to feel bad about, but [we’re] watching someone who was a real person [experiencing] the moment where [they have] a chance to stay real or move away from it.
That, hopefully, is the crux of the drama for us. Miller is now dangerous because he’s allowed his soul to be destroyed, and those are the people walking around in suits with nothing inside them we ought to really be frightened of. And yet, there was a way out for everyone. The pit in which the play is set is escapable, but some kinds of doom are self-imposed.
Christopher and Zachary, I have to imagine getting a script like this is very confronting. Christopher Dylan White : It was very frightening. It was a question of, “Am I even capable of doing what this play is asking me to do?” But I felt very seen by the script. What was on the page seemed to fulfill something that I had been dreaming about for a long time as an actor. [When I met] Zach, there was an instant chemistry and safety and respect that, when you’re dealing with a script like this, you would hope that you get. I was very lucky to find that.
Zachary Desmond : [The script] unlocked a thing in me as an actor just below the surface that was ready to be given air and space and oxygen. I just didn’t know I needed these particular facilitators to draw that out. They had been clear about who they were and that confirmation of “We want to see you erupt,” and I trusted that I’d find my way to understanding and [the ability to bring] so much love and care to [this character].
One of the things the play opened my eyes to is the incel-to-trans pipeline, which is the journey that Target takes. Else : I wouldn’t say in that order. Because of the way that masculinity destroys sort of everybody, it has different expressions, and the expressions that it has for repressing trans women, trans femmes, and incels are similar: It’s something about my immutable characteristics that make it so that I’m going to be unhappy in life . There’s a lot of similar expressions of misery, so they find themselves in similar spaces a lot of the time. But a lot of young trans people who are repressing or don’t understand it yet also have difficulty understanding sexuality because they don’t know how they want to be desired, which is very different from what they desire.
In terms of the performances of femininity and the abstractions of the idea of womanhood, Target is going from the almost grotesque, fetishized idea of a slur used against women and then, by degrees, comes closer and closer to embodying a femininity that actually makes sense for them.
But before that, the second act of the play climaxes in an especially in-your-face sex scene; in-your-face because you’re inches away from the front row. As actors, how do you get in the headspace for that? Emma : These freaks are fearless in similar ways. The way in which it was able to manifest physically was built on the foundation of their chemistry. The chemistry is the miracle sauce that makes the whole thing happen, but it’s not just a chemistry of vibe; it’s a chemistry of practice.
Christopher : Four years ago, Emma had us all take a breath before we started the work, where we allowed for the spirit of the play to enter the room. So, two hours into it, there was a safety to take the risk. Now, when we were working with Willow Funkhauser, who is an incredible choreographer and intimacy coordinator, she had us warm up with a series of—
Emma : Exercises about depth of touch: skin level, muscle level, bone level—
Christopher : And Zach and I felt it in our bodies and were able to approach each other. It was super informative to what we were going to build regarding the intimacy. There was a lot of careful consideration of each moment, and we also knew that we were going to build the whole thing and pare it down. But we didn’t [pare it down], because this is the story and it was honest. How do these people receive this thing that they’re claiming defines their inability to live their life now that they’re actually getting to experience it?
Zachary : The fact is that the play, as written and directed, is setting up [the idea that] eye contact is an enormous event that has real consequences on the bodies of these young people. The best part about that is the best part about what acting can be with a scene partner that you trust. I don’t know how to talk about chemistry, but what is happening on some level is that I’m stepping into a space, people are watching me look into the eyes of another person, and that person did, on the first day, really look back.
Any time that happens, it has a palpable magic. It has a molecule-changing effect on the people who are experiencing it. And then everything else is an expression of that effect. But it is the thing that happen

articles.title_orig: ‘Wow, dude. You’re an idiot’: why Kelly Clarkson is fighting over a $15,000 bird on social media
articles.title_zh: ‘Wow, dude. You’re an idiot’: why Kelly Clarkson is fighting over a $15,000 bird on social media
articles.content_orig:
After having a Pretty Woman moment in a Brooklyn store, the singer-songwriter let rip on X
Age: 44. Born in 1982. In Fort Worth, as it happens.
Is that relevant? Not really, but ask how much she’s worth.
How much is she worth? Celebritynetworth.com estimates the singer, songwriter and TV personality has a net worth of $60m.
Good for Clarkson. And is that relevant? Well, it just means she can afford stuff.
What kind of stuff? A $15,000 mechanical bird called Molly.
Great! So has she got one? No.
Why ever not? In Clarkson’s version of events, she visited a Brooklyn curiosity store, enquired about the bird and was treated like a Julia Roberts character.
Erin Brockovich ? Respect! No, Vivian Ward in Pretty Woman.
They thought she was on a “date ” with Richard Gere? No! But you’ll remember in the movie Roberts’s character is snubbed in a bijou Beverly Hills boutique. Clarkson says the same happened to her at Art of Play, where when she inquired about Molly, a member of staff looked at her “as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me”.
So she had a makeover and returned triumphantly to the store, just like in the movie? That was 1990, dear – Clarkson reacted the modern way.
Which is? She took to social media . “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” she posted on X, to her 8.8 million followers.
What did Art of Play do? Took to social media too, of course.
To apologise? Not really. “Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store,” they said on Instagram . They also said that Molly wasn’t even for sale.
Just a little misunderstanding, then, and all cleared up now? Hmm. “Sure, it wasn’t for sale,” said Clarkson. “So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag … didn’t happen … Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar.”
Ouch! She goes on to say she loves and supports small businesses: “I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t.”
No olive branch from Clarkson, then. What about the store? The Times reported that Art of Play said a worker told Clarkson that while Molly was not for sale, her “twin” made by an artist in Seattle was, for $15,000. They say they’ve reached out directly to try to clear the air. “We really do wish her the best and hope that someday we can all laugh about this misunderstanding.”
But we’re already laughing. Snobby shop, celebrity strop, a pile-on and a very expensive bird called Molly. True, what’s not to love?
Do say: “There’s a mechanical bird on Temu for £11.27.”

articles.title_orig: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI
articles.title_zh: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI
articles.content_orig:
Apple on Tuesday announced a new home hub called HomeView .
Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13.
Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music.
"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users.
Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.
But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus.
Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.
HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house.
Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as new boss Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.
Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and comes after a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable.

articles.title_orig: From Mongolia to the world: Rotary members mobilize for World Polio Day
articles.title_zh: From Mongolia to the world: Rotary members mobilize for World Polio Day
articles.content_orig:
As World Polio Day approaches, Rotary members around the world are mobilizing their communities to raise awareness, advocate for continued commitment and help make polio history.
In Mongolia, the World Polio Day season got off to an energetic start as around 200 members of Rotary, Rotaract and Interact clubs came together for a 3.5-kilometre End Polio Walk through the Mongolian National Park.
Organized by Areas 9 and 10 of Rotary District 3450, the event brought together Rotary members from across Mongolia, joined by District Deputy Secretary Joao Francisco Pinto, who travelled from Hong Kong to take part. Before setting off, participants warmed up together with Biyelgee, a traditional Mongolian dance – bringing a distinctly local flavour to a global cause.
And Mongolia is just the beginning.
In the weeks around World Polio Day on 24 October, Rotary members and partners will come together through events and activities across the globe – each different, but united behind the same goal.
At WHO headquarters in Geneva, WHO and Rotary will bring together Rotary members, Member States, polio survivors and eradication partners for a special event featuring WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and highlighting the extraordinary partnership that has brought the world to the threshold of eradication.
In Brussels, one of the city’s most famous residents will also join the effort: on 23 October, Manneken Pis will be dressed in a specially designed End Polio Now outfit, turning the iconic landmark into perhaps the world’s smallest polio eradication ambassador.
In London, parliamentarians and polio advocates will come together to keep political attention focused on finishing the job. And in Essen, Germany, Rotary members and partners will gather at the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Zollverein industrial complex to reflect on the progress made and the commitment still needed to make polio history.
These are just a few examples of activities taking place around the world – from community walks and public events to political advocacy, awareness campaigns and fundraising – demonstrating the unique role Rotary members continue to play in mobilizing communities and sustaining commitment to a polio-free world.
This year, people everywhere can also take part through the Team End Polio Challenge on Strava , turning their own walks, runs and rides into a show of support for polio eradication. Participants can also raise funds for Rotary’s PolioPlus Fund, helping support efforts to reach and protect children from polio.
Since launching PolioPlus more than four decades ago, Rotary has combined grassroots action with global advocacy and resource mobilization to help drive the world towards eradication. World Polio Day is an opportunity to celebrate that extraordinary progress – but also to remind the world that the job is not yet finished.
More than 99% of the way there is an extraordinary achievement. But when it comes to eradication, 99% is not enough.
From Mongolia to Geneva, Brussels, London and Essen – and in communities around the world – the message this World Polio Day is the same:  Together, we can make polio history.

Apple launched a new $299 Apple TV 4K streaming device today, with an upgraded chip, integration with the updated version of Siri AI for content discovery, and mics that allow users to issue voice commands directly without using the remote.
The refreshed Apple TV 4K comes with an upgraded A19 chip to enable various AI features. Hardware-wise, the new streaming box comes with three far-field microphones, letting users talk with Siri without a remote or a paired HomePod.
The company said that users can now have a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K  and HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2 speakers.
The remote also gets a welcome update: It now includes a small speaker. This helps users find the remote easily when it gets lost in the nooks and corners of the couch or when they leave the remote in another room while doing a chore. (Apple added a way to find the remote with Siri and Find My in 2023 , but it hinged on showing directions in the app rather than an audible sound.)
With Siri AI now rolling out to all Apple platforms, the big draw for Apple is to utilize it for better personalization and content recommendations. On the Apple TV, viewers can ask questions like “Which Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” to search for content, or ask for more information about shows with questions like “Where was ‘Pluribus’ filmed?”
Rivals Google and Amazon have also added AI for content suggestions in the past few years.
The device is not updated as often as other Apple hardware, given this long-pending upgrade comes four years after the launch of Apple TV 4K in 2022. Bloomberg reported that the company wanted to launch the new device in 2024, but delays in launching the AI-powered Siri forced Apple to push the launch of new home devices as well.
Consumers can preorder the new Apple TV 4K starting today, and the device will be available on November 13.

articles.title_orig: U.K. intelligence chief warns Iran is shifting plots to ‘harder targets’
articles.title_zh: U.K. intelligence chief warns Iran is shifting plots to ‘harder targets’
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
LONDON — Iran is trying to hit military sites in Britain and the suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run military air base in September is “not unique,” the head of the MI5 spy agency said Tuesday, as he warned that both Tehran and Moscow are expanding their attacks against the U.K.
Ken McCallum, who leads the U.K.’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities.
That has included arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites that Britain says were carried out by Iranian proxies.
McCallum said another “major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”
The incident at RAF Fairford “is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the U.K. but around the world,” McCallum said.
McCallum delivered his annual speech outlining major threats to the U.K. as counterterror detectives investigate a suspected terror plot against the U.S.-run base in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year’s war.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
Seven men in their 20s have been arrested and released on bail under investigation. In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, or IRGC. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
The U.S. pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, and the Trump administration said it believed the base faced Iranian threats intended to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible.
British officials have not confirmed that, and McCallum said that, in the U.K., Iran has so far used low-level criminal proxies who lack the capacity to mount a sophisticated large-scale attack. But he said Iran’s IRGC has shown stronger capabilities in countries closer to Iran, “so it would be foolish for a person in a role like mine to discount the possibility.”
In a stark speech, McCallum argued that the U.K. faces a “new era of national security,” with a generational shift equivalent to the 9/11 attacks a quarter century ago. He said the myriad threats to national security now range from “arson, sabotage cyberattacks, coercion, violence” to “what online algorithms are feeding your teenagers in their bedrooms.”
McCallum said his agency’s work countering state threats – chiefly from Russia, Iran and China – has quadrupled in the past decade, and claimed that both Russia and Iran are escalating hybrid warfare campaigns against the U.K. and other European countries.
He said Russia has been linked to attacks including an attempt to use an explosives-laden drone at Germany’s Leipzig airport, and is “using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict.”
Meanwhile, technology is racing ahead, with artificial intelligence “supercharging” the cybersecurity battle between attackers and defenders, he said.
McCallum said terror plotters have used artificial intelligence for reconnaissance and attacks, including AI-enabled drones. Even more concerning, he said, is “AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons.”
After the speech he told journalists at MI5’s London headquarters that terror groups “would dearly love” to have chemical, biological or radiological weapons, but these are hard to obtain.
“One risk is that AI could enable dangerous knowledge to get into the hands of people we would all rather didn’t have that knowledge,” he said. “A second and different risk … is the possibility that AI could generate novel pathogens not previously seen.”
McCallum said MI5 has set up a new AI Threat Assessment Center to try to keep ahead of the risks.
“Human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. It is capable of outthinking us. This is genuinely novel, and deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5,” he said.
Lawless writes for the Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania announces sixth death in measles outbreak as case numbers rise
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania announces sixth death in measles outbreak as case numbers rise
articles.content_orig:
Latest fatality is unvaccinated woman, 39, with ‘underlying conditions’ but CDC still lists only two deaths nationwide
A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania ’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100.
The most recent fatality was reported in Franklin county on Monday in a statement posted to Facebook by its coroner. The victim was identified as a 39-year-old female who “had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment”.
The coroner, James Conner, said it was the first measles-related death in the county “for many years” – and that the patient’s recent diagnosis met the definition of the Pennsylvania health department for inclusion.
Five other people have died after contracting measles since August in Pennsylvania, which state officials said on Monday had now recorded 1,137 cases and 219 hospitalizations. The outbreak began west of Philadelphia in April, with authorities blaming low vaccination rates.
The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, continues to list deaths nationally at two amid a dispute between the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy, and Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over the methodology for classifying measles-related fatalities.
The CDC’s website , last updated on Friday, shows 4,080 confirmed measles infections across the US in 42 separate outbreaks, the highest figures in decades, and almost double the number of cases for the whole of 2025.
Earlier in October, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared an emergency because of rising case numbers in her state; while Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Utah have also seen significant increases.
A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of the Franklin county fatality – and was “conducting a thorough review of the reported death”.
The coroner’s office told the outlet through a spokesperson that the woman’s “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles”. The coroner’s office spokesperson said the woman was not vaccinated.
Conner’s statement did not identify the woman to protect the privacy of the victim and relatives. “Families deserve the dignity to mourn in private,” that statement said.
“We strongly encourage our medical community, first responders, and the public to follow the precautions set forth by” Pennsylvania state guidelines.
Those state guidelines recommend two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine, or a combined MMRV vaccine including varicella (chickenpox) protection for children 12 and older.
The CDC website recommends the same vaccinations, but Kennedy – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has offered mixed messages. In March 2025, he questioned the effectiveness of the measles vaccine, saying people should be able “to make that choice for themselves ” about whether to take it.
And in September, he told anti-vaccine activists at a conference in Washington DC that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House”, a month after telling US families in response to the rise in measles cases nationwide that parents “ should get their children vaccinated ”.
The Pennsylvania outbreak has seen 157 new cases over the last week, state figures showed, and one-third of the overall number of infections have come in those 18 or under. Fewer than 1% of cases occurred in those who are fully vaccinated.
The first two fatalities, reported in August, were infants, one whose mother had measles during her pregnancy, and the second a six-week-old who also had a rare genetic condition.
The other Pennsylvania victims were women aged 40 and 20, and an 18-year-old, all of whom had coexisting health conditions.
