articles.title_orig: In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026
articles.title_zh: In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026
articles.content_orig:
In exactly a month, on November 13, 2026, the world will end. Fittingly, our impending apocalypse falls on Friday the 13th .
At least, that was the prediction made by University of Illinois physicist Heinz von Foerster in a highly cited Science paper published in 1960. Though talks of supposed doomsday have renewed in recent months thanks to hyperbolic anxieties over runaway, sentient artificial intelligence, von Foerster had a much different calamity in mind.
For more than a century, the prevailing fear, dating back to English economist Thomas Malthus who lived between 1766 to 1834, was of a booming population outrunning its food supply. Famine would ensue. But Von Foerster broke from that view. He assumed (correctly, as it turns out) that human ingenuity would keep the world mostly fed. The problem, he argued, was that the population would keep accelerating, toward “infinity.”
In a now infamous quote, von Foerster predicted, “Our great—great—grandchildren will not starve to death,” von Foerster and his co-authors wrote. “They will be squeezed to death.” Homo sapiens’ last gasping breath, they predicted, would peter out in the fall of 2026.
It’s pretty clear that von Foerster’s estimate was dead wrong. Not only is the global population ( around 8.3 billion people ) not expanding near the rate it was when he was writing, but there are actually concerns it’s moving in the opposite direction . In dozens of countries around the world, from South Korea and Japan to much of Western Europe, the concern among demographers has shifted from worries about overpopulation to declining birth rates.
In the United States, President Donald Trump has jumped on the issue, calling himself the “ fertilization president ” offering tax incentives for new families and even exploring medals for women who give birth to six or more children. Joseph Stalin previously championed that last idea.
So how was a prediction so wrong and still so influential? Human population experts speaking with Popular Science say von Foerster and his contemporaries based their prediction on real trends from the past while utterly failing to see the world changing right before their eyes. Though they may have accurately measured growth rates up to that point, that only tells part of the story.
“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” Rockefeller University and Columbia University professor and mathematical biologist Joel Cohen tells Popular Science. Cohen has studied human population changes for years and published the influential 1995 book How Many People Can the Earth Support?
“Von Foerster didn’t know at the time, and in fact, nobody knew” that the all-time population growth had already happened, Cohen adds. “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.”
Von Foerster and his colleagues published their “Doomsday” paper on November 4, 1960. The dramatic pronouncement hinges on an equation that projects the human population into the future based on past trends.
The team gathered 24 estimates of world population dating back 2,000 years. The key assumption underpinning their logic was that humans differ from other animals because of our unique ability to cooperate and innovate.
Fruit flies in a jar eventually level off as crowding and competition take their toll. Humans, on the other hand, the authors argue, work the other way. The more of us there are, the better we get at cooperating. And the better we get at cooperation, the faster our population grows.
Follow that curve forward, and the population doesn’t just grow; it rockets toward infinity, hitting the so-called mathematical wall on November 13, 2026, give or take five years.
Von Foerster wasn’t alone in sounding the alarm either. Eight years later, biologist Paul R. Ehrlich would publish The Population Bomb , arguably the most influential single text fueling overpopulation fears.
“Both of those guys were right looking backward, but wrong looking forward,” Cohen says.
At a glance, thinking the future will resemble the past seems pretty reasonable. The human population grew steadily but slowly over much of our roughly 300,000 years of humanity. But that changed radically with the onset of globalization, colonization, and the Industrial Revolution.
As Darrell Bricker and John Ibbitson note in their 2020 book Empty Planet: The Shock of Global Population Decline , human population passed the one billion mark somewhere around 1800. That doubled to two billion by 1927. Then doubled again just less than 50 years later in 1974. It would then only take another 13 years to cross the five billion mark. And in 2022, we surpassed eight billion.
That remarkable explosion had many causes, Cohen says, but among the most important was the spread of cheap, calorie-dense crops like potatoes and corn from the Americas.
Crucially, though, humans weren’t necessarily having way more kids. They were just far better at keeping them alive.
“Humanity got better at keeping the people who were born alive through simple, but important innovations like the germ theory of disease, sanitation, nutrition,” University of Texas Associate professor and economic demographer Dean Spears tells Popular Science.
Demographers like Spears study human populations and how they change over time. He published a book on the topic titled After the Spike , earlier this year. Advances in nutrition and medicine “caused early life mortality rates to fall, so more of the humans who were born survived and that caused the population to grow.”
Factoring in longer life expectancy and reductions in child mortality around the world blows a huge hole in Von Foerster’s calculations. Death rates can only fall so far, and once most children survive, families tend to have fewer of them.
The population boom was a one time explosion, not an ever-accelerating loop.
Von Foerster’s assumption of endlessly accelerating growth, Spears says, was “based on a misunderstanding of where population growth comes from.”
Experts specializing in human population studies at the time actually knew that was the case, Spears notes.
Neither von Foerster’s nor Ehrlich (who wrote The Population Bomb) were human population experts. Von Foerster’s background was in physics and philosophy. Ehrlich was a biologist. But they were both great at getting attention.
Indeed, academics at the time reportedly sent flustered letters to the editor at Science , calling the prediction “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.”
“There was never, even at that time, any reason to think that it would keep growing fast like that.” Spears says. “Paul Ehrlich was a biologist who studied butterflies , not human demography.”
In the later 20th century, population growth actually started declining quite rapidly thanks to a convergence of a variety of factors.
The “Green Revolution” in farming meant that more food could be grown on the same plot of land, which extinguished fears of humanity suddenly starving itself. The first birth control pill , approved by the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) in the U.S. in 1957 , also gave women more autonomy to decide when and how many children to have.
These trends, along with global population shifts away from rural areas and towards more urban areas, would eventually shift concerns away from overpopulation and towards declining birth rates.
Although demographers and policy experts debate how much people should worry about declining birth rates, it is generally agreed that an older population that significantly outnumbers younger people can lead to long-term strains on the country’s economy and social services.
With fewer workers needed in the field, more and more people moved to cities. Historically, families living on farms or agricultural communities tend to have more children than those in urban areas because those children could work the land and, in a purely economic sense, provide more labor and, hopefully, make the family more money. articles.title_orig: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim
articles.title_zh: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge in New York on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt, alleging he "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 civil court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry.
The FTC and the states allege that Shkreli, since being released from prison in May 2022 for unrelated financial crimes, violated that court order by publicly trading in at least 60 pharmaceutical industry stocks and "publicly broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of many Pharmaceutical Companies through livestreaming and posting on numerous social media platforms, including YouTube, X, and Reddit," a court filing says.
The contempt filing asks a judge to order Shkreli to "divest any pharmaceutical company stocks he currently owns" and "pay a fine equal to his profits from any pharmaceutical company stock trading (plus prejudgment interest) without the ability to account for offsetting losses."
The filing in U.S. District Court in Manhattan also asks that a judge make Shkreli "face clear and escalating consequences for any future violations, including financial penalties and potential incarceration."
FTC Commissioner Mark Meador said in a statement, "A lifetime industry ban is only effective if breaches are met with consequences commensurate with the seriousness of the order."
The court order stems from a finding that Shkreli organized an anti-competitive scheme to perpetuate his company Vyera Pharmaceuticals' monopoly in the anti-parasitic drug Daraprim. Shkreli had hiked the price of Daraprim from $17.50 per tablet to a whopping $750 per pill.
In addition to banning him from the drug industry for life, a judge ordered Shkreli to disgorge more than $64 million. The 2nd Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals upheld the permanent injunction against Shkreli in January 2024, and the Supreme Court declined to take his appeal of the order in October 2024.
CNBC has requested comment from an attorney for Shkreli.
In addition to the FTC, the states that joined Tuesday's court filing are New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
The filing asks the judge to order Shkreli's sister, Leonora Izerne, and his "significant other, Chelsea Voss," to preserve all evidence relating to potential violations of the injunction against Shkreli because both women "appear to have assisted or be assisting Shkreli in violating the Permanent Injunction."
The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. Shkreli was sentenced to seven years in federal prison in 2018, and was released in 2022 with credit for time locked up before he was sentenced and other factors.
"After a full trial, the court found that Martin Shkreli's conduct drove up prescription drug costs for American patients and blocked the entry of lower-cost generics,"Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC's Bureau of Competition, said in a statement on Tuesday.
"When judgment is entered by a court, whether it's a settlement or an order following a trial, defendants must fulfill their obligations," Guarnera said. "Today's action should serve as notice that the FTC will not hesitate to enforce violations of court orders."

articles.content_orig:

Growth at Punta Cana Air Cargo Hub, new European connections, and economic zone development at Caucedo create new options for businesses across the Americas
SANTO DOMINGO, Dominican Republic, Oct. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- DP World is expanding its integrated logistics and manufacturing platform in the Dominican Republic, combining growing air cargo connectivity with new manufacturing and logistics capacity to connect businesses across the Americas with global markets.
The strategy brings together DP World's operations at the Port of Caucedo with the Punta Cana Air Cargo Hub and new manufacturing and logistics capacity, strengthening the Dominican Republic's role as a gateway for trade across the Americas.
DP World executives discussed the development of the multimodal platform during the XLVIII Port Meeting of the Central American Isthmus (REPICA) 2026, which brought together nearly 400 participants from more than 14 countries.
Roberto Muñiz, Commercial Director of DP World in the Dominican Republic, said: "The role of ports is evolving. Today, competitiveness depends not only on moving cargo efficiently, but on connecting transportation, logistics, and manufacturing within an integrated ecosystem. Our investments are designed to give companies more options to manufacture, distribute and connect with international markets from the Dominican Republic."
Expanding air cargo connectivity
The Punta Cana Air Cargo Hub – a joint development between DP World and the Punta Cana Free Trade Zone (PCFTZ), a subsidiary of Grupo Puntacana – began operations in late 2023 , creating a regional gateway for time-sensitive and high-value cargo. In 2025, the hub handled more than 33,000 tones of import, export and transit cargo, up 15% from the previous year.
Earlier this year, DP World and PCFTZ added twice-weekly connections to Europe , linking cargo from South America, Central America and the Caribbean with key European markets, including Madrid, Frankfurt and London.
With approximately 4,000 square meters of cold storage capacity, the hub supports perishables, pharmaceuticals, parcels and other high-value cargo, providing regional exporters with additional routes to international markets.
Expanding manufacturing and logistics capacity
DP World is also advancing the next phase of its economic zone expansion at the Port of Caucedo, creating additional capacity for companies seeking to manufacture, assemble and distribute products from the Dominican Republic.
In 2025, DP World signed a multimillion-dollar Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of the Dominican Republic to expand the Port of Caucedo and its adjacent Free Trade Zone. The planned development would increase annual container-handling capacity from 2.5 million TEUs to approximately 3.1 million TEUs and unlock 225 hectares of development-ready land for manufacturing, logistics and advanced services.
For more insights into how DP World is reshaping global trade, visit our website: www.dpworld.com
For media enquiries, please contact:
Melina Vissat, Head of Communications M: (+1) 704-605-6159 E: melina.vissat@dpworld.com
DP World is reshaping the future of global trade to improve lives everywhere. Operating across six continents with a team of over 125,000 employees, we combine global infrastructure and local expertise to deliver seamless supply chain solutions. From Ports and Terminals to Marine Services, Logistics and Technology, we leverage innovation to create better ways to trade, minimizing disruptions from the factory floor to the customer's door.
In the Americas, DP World operates with a team of over 16,000 people across 12 countries, driving excellence through a robust network of 14 ports and terminals and more than 40 warehouses. By harnessing our global reach and local expertise, we simplify logistics, enhance operational performance, and redefine the boundaries of what's possible in global trade.

articles.title_orig: New search begins for Amelia Earhart plane suspected to be buried in lagoon
articles.title_zh: New search begins for Amelia Earhart plane suspected to be buried in lagoon
articles.content_orig:
A team of researchers have arrived at a remote island to inspect possible plane wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart, who vanished in 1937 while flying around the world.
The group from the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University arrived at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean on Monday.
The search team's work, expected to take five days, could be hampered by giant land-dwelling crabs, as well as the El Niño climate phenomenon which is now the strongest ever recorded .
Coconut crabs, also known as Robber crabs, emerge at night to hunt for small mammals and seabirds, and will force the search crew to spend nights on their ship for their own safety.
The disappearance of Earhart, an American aviation pioneer who was attempting to circumnavigate the globe with navigator Fred Noonan, has spawned decades of speculation.
Researchers will work to locate what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.
Some believe it to be the wreckage of her plane, but others have expressed scepticism that it is an aircraft at all, with one theory suggesting it is a collapsed tree.
This is the first authorised trip to Nikumaroro Island in seven years, and the first visit to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15, according to Purdue.
The ship, the Marin Mainiku, on Monday arrived at the western side of the island, part of the nation of Kiribati, after a five-day voyage crossing 830-nautical-miles through the South Pacific.
"It is incredibly rewarding to be this close to completing our inspection of the Taraia Object and potentially solving, at long last, the outstanding mystery of the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan more than 89 years ago," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said in a blog post on Monday.
On Tuesday, the crew plans to navigate through a narrow gap "blasted" in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited - to prepare for landing.
The first day on the island will focus on "transporting equipment, clearing vegetation, and establishing staging operations", according to the post. One group of researchers will cut a trail through the jungle.
Work will then shift to searching for evidence, including magnetic metals, on the Taraia Peninsula on Wednesday.
Lastly, the researchers will use dredging equipment to move sediment for a visual inspection of the mystery object, which is believed to be located only 10 feet from the shore in as little as five feet of water (depending on the tides).
Weather and ocean conditions "will continue to be a factor", researchers say, and El Niño could limit daily access to shore. Michael Krivor, a marine archaeologist on the trip, said he is currently concerned about a weather pattern traveling from east to west that could interfere with "safe transit in and out of the blasted channels".
Another concern is the crabs, the largest land-dwelling invertebrates on the planet.
"The crew will sleep nightly aboard the Marin Mainiku for a number of reasons, one of which is the presence of coconut crabs, whose size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical," the blog post says.
Several theories suggest  Earhart survived a crash on the island before being overcome by giant meat-eating crabs that carried away her bones.
The crabs, which occupy atolls and desert islands throughout the South Pacific, can lift up to 28kg (62lbs), and are one of the only species that can crack open a coconut, although they also hunt for live prey like rats and birds.
With a leg span of up to one metre and a body weight of more than 4kg, they are also the world's largest land-dwelling crustacean and are able to climb trees.
In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery used pig carcasses to demonstrate how the crabs were able to drag bodies to their burrows and strip the bones of flesh in less than two weeks.
Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea, on 2 July 1937.
From there, she and Noonan planned to travel towards Hawaii, but the plane vanished without a trace as they tried to reach uninhabited Howland Island, near Nikumaroro, to refuel.
While there have been numerous theories about the disappearance, the official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems and, as she and Noonan struggled to find the island, the plane ran out of fuel and crashed into the ocean.

articles.title_orig: Heathrow's Northern Runway has tarmac replaced in overnight works
articles.title_zh: Heathrow's Northern Runway has tarmac replaced in overnight works
articles.content_orig:
We are waiting for the last plane to leave Heathrow.
It is 10:45pm and we are in a convoy of road maintenance vehicles on the edge of the Northern Runway.
We see the plane take off. The call comes through on the radio and 130 vehicles head to the tarmac.
It reminds me of the cartoon Wacky Races, with all vehicles of different shapes and sizes speeding down the runway. The race is now on to replace it.
I have been given exclusive access to see the work. They have just five hours to do a section. Planes with passengers on board are already on their way from the US, Australia or the Far East to land here.
It is an incredible sight. There are 230 specialist workers who soon jump out of the vehicles, set up cones and measure lines. Then, within 10 minutes, the road millers start tearing up the surface.
The clock is ticking and the pressure is on.
The runway needs replacing as there is 10kg of plane tyre rubber embedded into the surface. The work is noisy. There is no pause between each type of work.
Heathrow's infrastructure delivery and strategic planning director is Alistair Awcock.
He is well aware of how important this job is.
"It's a scheme that we undertake about every sort of 10 - 12 years, based on the condition of the runway," said Awcock.
"Obviously, our runways are our most critical asset, it is the thing that keeps our business operating. So, we're willing to invest to make sure that this stays operational all year round.
"It is a big job. Every night our team come out over the whole of the summer, a three-month period, and resurface about 75 metres (246ft) of runway every night."
So how do they do it? Gawaine Yates is the delivery project manager.
"We've carefully planned this work. This team have practised this over and over again and fine-tuned it. This is a skill, they're specialist teams."
He said the old surface is taken off and recycled into making local roads or used in the construction industry.
"Once they've taken all of this material out, we will be ready to start preparing the surface for the new asphalt.
"Because we're creating a hole in Heathrow's most critical asset, we have to make sure that all of the asphalt is back."
The construction team needs the asphalt to be an exact thickness and type and to be ready exactly when they need it.
"We started mixing asphalt at 19:00 hours tonight. On site, we have two [mixers] back in plants at the south side of the airfield.
"Twenty-five wagons will bring the lower layer, and then once they've laid that, the wagons will all go right down to the southern end of the airfield again, and collect the next 500 tonnes worth of material to do our surface course material.
"Once that's all compacted and sealed, cooling will take place between the layers, and then once it's cool enough, we will apply the new paint markings."
This is one of the busiest runways in the world.
There are around 1,300 combined take-offs and landings a day at Heathrow. Most aircraft weigh around 200 tonnes, travelling about 140mph when touching down.
Gawaine Yates says the crews are well aware of the pressure.
They need to set up a construction site, do the work and be ready to leave at 04:30 so the operations team can carry out a foreign object debris inspection to ensure the runway is safe in time for 06:00 when the first plane lands.
"The logistics is very challenging. As far as laying asphalt, it's fairly standard, the sort of thing you see on the roads. It's just in a more concentrated scale. It's a much more difficult material to lay than the highways."
So what if they fall behind or there is a problem?
"Everybody knows what they're doing. It's a very busy site, but they do this repetitively. We've practised it, we've run trials on it, and they've been learning on this to improve shift by shift."
"There's a lot to be done in a short window. If anything goes wrong, they feel that pressure.
"We have a heavy recovery truck on site every single night, in case one of these bits of equipment breaks down. That's a very rare occurrence, but we have to make sure that we can get that back off the runway."
By the end of the year, the project will have replaced around 200,000 tonnes of asphalt. Some construction jobs are deemed a success if no-one notices it. This is one of them.
Gawaine Yates says so far it has gone well.
"That's what we've been striving to do. We've not had a single late handback.
"The public have not known any dramas from here, because we're dealing with it on the night.
"We have resilience built into the shift, so that everybody knows what they're doing.
"If something goes wrong, we've done exercises to make sure that we can get back on track and deliver that handover by the absolute crystal latest... 05:30.
"We have to be, everybody done and dusted, ready to give it back to air traffic control, at 05:45, to vector that first aircraft into the runway at 06:00."
Any delay in the work would have serious consequences, Awcock said.
"Fingers crossed, we haven't had any operational issues.
"The implications of not handing back this runway to our operation is not just an impact to Heathrow but would impact the whole of the UK airspace."

articles.title_orig: These are the world's best cruise lines and ships for 2026
articles.title_zh: These are the world's best cruise lines and ships for 2026
articles.content_orig:
The winners of the World Cruise Awards have just been revealed for 2026 – and Norwegian Cruise Line has taken the top prize.
Now in its sixth edition, the winners were announced on 12 October at a gala ceremony in Jamaica.
Norwegian Cruise Line was named the world’s best cruise line for 2026, beating out nominees including MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean International and Silversea.
As for where you should be going for your next voyage, the UAE’s capital Abu Dhabi was named the world’s best cruise destination. It should be noted that some cruise lines have revised their 2026/27 schedules to avoid Gulf ports, given the ongoing crisis in the region.
Lisbon was the only European destination among the nominees’ list, which also included Auckland Island in New Zealand, Jamaica, Mexico, Morocco, Prince Edward Island in Canada, the Seychelles and Vietnam.
For those who have Patagonia on their bucket list, you should be looking to book with Australis, which was named the world’s best expedition cruise line.
Thinking about a river cruise ? Pandaw, which operates throughout countries in Asia including India, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, was named the world’s best river cruise line.
Which is handy, because Vietnam was also named the world’s best river cruise destination.
Within Europe, DouroAzul was named the best river cruise line, while Lisbon in Portugal was selected as the best river cruise destination.
The World Cruise Awards also hand out gongs to individual cruise ships under categories such as dining, families and romance.
For foodies, the best cruise ship is Sun Princess, which has seven specialty restaurants. These include American steakhouse Crown Grill, Sabatini's Italian Trattoria, seafood spot The Catch by Rudi (Sodamin, the cruise line’s head of culinary arts), The Butcher's Block by Dario (Cecchini, an eighth generation Italian butcher), show-stopping Umai Teppanyaki, sushi eatery Makoto Ocean, and Umai Hot Pot.
If you’re travelling with your little ones, Disney Wish was named the best option for families, for obvious reasons.
Expect live shows themed around classics like The Little Mermaid and Aladdin, restaurants that will transport you to Frozen’s Arendelle or the world of Marvel, plus water slides, sports courts and a movie theatre. Big kids won’t miss out on the fun, either, with cocktail bars, pubs, a spa, and an adults-only refuge with an infinity pool.
Celebrity Apex was selected as the world’s best cruise for romance. Here, you can relax by the adults-only Solarium pool, catch a live performance with a cocktail at the cantilevered, floating platform The Magic Carpet, or play games together at The Casino.
If you want a cruise ship that will keep you entertained even between ports, try Utopia of the Seas.
On board, there are five pools, three water slides, 21 restaurants and 23 bars (including a karaoke spot), two casinos and plenty of shows, whether you’re into comedy or live music.

articles.title_orig: He Would Be Florida’s First Black Governor. Can He Sway Black Voters?
articles.title_zh: He Would Be Florida’s First Black Governor. Can He Sway Black Voters?
articles.content_orig:
TALLAHASSEE — A Black Democrat and a white Republican, both women, are vying to be U.S. Senator from Florida. The governor’s bout has the opposite, and far more unusual, configuration: white male Democrat vs. Black male Republican.
And that has led to striking if sometimes subtle stylistic and rhetorical differences in how race is playing in these two top-of-the-ticket contests.
Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat from urban Jacksonville, faces Ashley Moody, the former state attorney general appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to fill out the remainder of Marco Rubio’s senate term.
In the governors’ race, Byron Donalds, a GOP congressman from mostly white suburban Naples is running against David Jolly, a former Republican congressman turned Democrat from Indian Shores, a beachside community in Pinellas County.
While Nixon leans into the issues that affect Black voters, Donalds, an early favorite with his endorsement from President Trump, eschewed Black political events and specific issues for most of his campaign, focusing on broader concerns like economic growth and school choice.
That’s a reflection of a difficult reality for Black candidates, especially in a Southern state, experts say: Progressives may motivate their base by engaging on race, but conservatives risk alienating their core supporters.
“Usually, when a Black candidate is running for state or national office in a predominantly white environment they downplay race, and don’t talk about race unless they have to,” University of Florida political science professor Sharon Wright Austin said.
But Donalds seemed to shift that stance in the last few weeks as recent polls show him running neck and neck with Jolly, who has overwhelming support among Black voters even though Donald is the first Black Republican nominee for governor and could become Florida’s first Black Governor.
Donalds only has 10-14% support among Blacks compared to Jolly’s 76-83% support in various surveys.
“Donalds knows that MAGA base may not be enough,” Austin said.
But, she said, “If he tries to talk to the Black voters, he will turn off the people in his base.”
And that is why he mostly sticks to “deracialized issues” like the economy and educational opportunities, she said.
Donalds also doesn’t have much support among rural white Republican voters, especially in the more “Dixie-fied” parts of the state, which at least some observers believe may connect to race.
It’s easy to assert that “Donalds is suffering some sort of racist electoral penalty … but kind of hard to prove, at least in advance,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a weekly political analysis newsletter published by the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia.
“I can totally see Donalds underperforming in North Florida,” said Matt Isbell, a Democratic political consultant who specializes in analyzing voter turnout.
But North Florida does not determine the outcome of an election the way South Florida does, Isbell said.
“If Donalds is to lose it won’t be because of the people in Lafayette County, it will be because moderate suburban Republicans are unhappy with the economy,” Isbell said.
In recent weeks, Donalds has focused more on the Black community  – appearing at a historically Black college for the first time, meeting with leaders in South Florida’s Caribbean community and announcing a panel of mostly conservative Black leaders to assist with community outreach. Donalds appeared on Oct. 3, as did Jolly, at Onyx Magazine’s Men of Honor Gala at Rosen Centre Hotel in Orlando.
Donalds has also received the endorsement of Cynthia Moore Chestnut, a prominent Black Democrat and former state representative who currently sits on the Gainesville City Commission.
But most Blacks are wary of Donalds, largely because of his support of Trump and national GOP policies that seem like an existential threat to the future well-being and progress of Blacks, said Bruce Strouble, a political science professor at Florida A&M University.
“He doesn’t seem to speak to the issues of Black people, but policies that white Republican elitists like,” Strouble said.
Donalds voted for Trump’s so-called “Big Beautiful Bill Act” last year, which slashed over $1 trillion in social programs but included tax breaks for the wealthy.
He also opposed expanding protections for voters, and supported efforts to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs and Black studies programs. And he supports Trump’s immigration policies, which pose trouble for many of the close to 160,000 Haitians living in Florida.
During a town hall meeting last month at Florida A&M University in Tallahassee, students sparred with Donalds over immigration, critical race theory, gun safety and the state’s diversity policies. Donalds, a former FAMU student himself, fired back by criticizing students for blindly voting for Democrats.
“I’m just gonna be blunt: stop moving like a monolith,” he said.
Strouble, who attended the meeting, said students came in wanting to learn more about Donalds, but “the more he talked the more they realized his ideas will hurt their futures.”
Political consultant Nikki Barnes noted that Donalds changes his own story, depending on the audience.
“When he is in front of a white audience, the story is about self sufficiency, independence, and pulling himself up by his bootstraps,” Barnes posted on social media. But when he gets in front of Black students, Barnes said, he talks about being raised by a single mother.
Unlike Donalds, Nixon is taking heat for her refusal to moderate her views or her rhetoric. Nixon has been called a “ghetto b—-,” has been ridiculed over her hairstyle, her wardrobe and her southern accent, and has faced political backlash for joining the Democratic Socialist Party.
Nixon trails Moody by 10 percentage points in the latest Mason-Dixon poll, with white voters supporting Moody 61% to 29% and Blacks supporting Nixon 81% to 10%.
“She recognizes she needs white votes,” Strouble said of Nixon. So she is pushing policies that help an entire economic class of people, whites and people of color. “It’s a class solidarity campaign,” he said.  “White working class voters are realizing GOP policies aren’t working for them. It is a bold strategy. We will see if it works.”
Nixon is running the same kind of grassroots campaign she ran in the primary, where she defied expectations and defeated Alex Vindman, who outspent her 17 to 1.
She is going into rural white communities, another area where she outperformed Vindman in the primaries. She’s also emphasizing pocketbook issues, like inflation and gas prices. But she doesn’t limit herself to those issues.
“Nixon also doesn’t dance around the race issue, she calls it like she sees it,” Austin said.
When, during a campaign stop for Donalds, Vice President J.D. Vance said she should leave America, Nixon punched back.
“Imagine standing on the shoulders of the people who built this country & then telling their descendants they don’t belong here,” Nixon posted on social media.
Nixon has a chance of winning because “she is confronting the dog whistles openly,” Austin said.
“It would be erroneous to say she is not the underdog,” Austin said, “but if the people who want her to win turn out, she can win.”

articles.title_orig: Utah’s ‘world’s longest art gallery’ could see 500 oil trucks a day. A new lawsuit aims to stop that.
articles.title_zh: Utah’s ‘world’s longest art gallery’ could see 500 oil trucks a day. A new lawsuit aims to stop that.
articles.content_orig:
(Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance) Gate Canyon with a winding dirt road that would be straighten and paved under a plan approved by the Bureau of Land Management.
Note to readers • This story is made possible through a partnership between The Salt Lake Tribune and Grist , a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Environmental groups are suing the federal government over plans to blast a “ hydrocarbon highway ” through a Utah canyon full of cultural, archaeological and historical resources.
The Trump administration resurrected the project in Nine Mile Canyon in eastern Utah after it stalled out during President Joe Biden’s term. Environmental and historic preservation groups say approvals for the highway bypassed the normal public comment and ecological review processes. The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and Center for Biological Diversity filed a lawsuit against the Department of Interior and Bureau of Land Management on Oct. 6 to stop the project.
“It’s like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum,” J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, said in a statement.
(Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance) A Native American rock art panel in Nine Mile Canyon near Price.
The BLM’s website refers to Nine Mile as the “world’s longest art gallery” due to its extensive ancient petroglyphs, Native American panels and Pioneer-era axle-grease inscriptions. Nine Mile Canyon covers about 46 miles, and Gate Canyon has 47 historic sites with 43 eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, according to BLM documentation from 2015.
A BLM spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit.
The federal agency began considering plans to realign Gate Canyon’s winding dirt Wells Draw Road in 2015. Duchesne County sought a more direct route from the oil fields in the Uinta Basin to the rail facilities of Carbon County. The project could bring up to 500 heavy trucks through Nine Mile Canyon per day . Duchesne County has also said straightening the old county road would provide for safer travel.
In 2016, the BLM received nearly 700 public comments sharing concerns about impacts to Nine Mile Canyon from the increased traffic, the agency noted in its latest assessment.
The proposed highway would run 5.3 miles through lands owned by both the Bureau of Land Management and Utah’s Trust Lands Administration, although most of the switchbacks the highway project would straighten occur on state land.
(Bureau of Land Management) A proposed realignment of Wells Draw Road that would create a "hydrocarbon highway" between the oilfields of the Uinta Basin and the rail facilities of Carbon County.
The BLM paused its earlier environmental assessment of the project, the lawsuit claims, but it solicited public comments again in 2023 after reviewing an amended right-of-way that covers 2.8 miles running through federal lands. The highway proposal was again hit by a round of opposition. The plan was scrapped, with BLM citing the need for further cultural surveys and reports.
But a Duchesne County special service district submitted a new development plan in September 2025, which they finalized on April 13 of this year. The BLM approved it on April 28 after determining the highway “will not significantly affect” the environment, recreation, wildlife or quality of life.
In their lawsuit , the environmental groups disagreed with that assessment.
“The road construction will facilitate increased traffic through Gate Canyon and the adjoining Nine Mile Canyon, threatening some of the state’s most important cultural and scenic values in the larger Nine Mile Canyon region,” the lawsuit said.
Although the BLM issued a final environmental assessment in April, the environmental groups said the agency violated several federal laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The Gate Canyon project area potentially includes habitat for the threatened Mexican spotted owl, according to the agency’s own 2015 draft environmental assessment, environmental groups argued.
And despite that previous draft assessment identifying dozens of sites within Gate Canyon that are eligible for the National Register, including 11 “within feet” of the existing dirt road, the parties say the BLM signed off on the project without identifying any historical or archaeological resources.
The plaintiffs said they asked for public comment periods and to participate in the NEPA process after learning of the highway’s new development plan in March, but that the BLM either did not respond or denied those requests.
“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” said Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity. “We’re going to court to protect this irreplaceable cultural treasure and the animals calling it home.”
The federal government has not yet filed a response with the Utah District Court.

articles.title_orig: Leap seconds have righted global clocks 27 times. So why do timekeepers want to kill it?
articles.title_zh: Leap seconds have righted global clocks 27 times. So why do timekeepers want to kill it?
articles.content_orig:
When the sun hits its highest point over the meridian line that travels north and south from the 351-year-old Royal Observatory Greenwich in London, it’s noon Greenwich Mean Time, a tangible and physical reference point that helped establish the world’s time zone system.
Timekeeping has long relied on Earth’s spin and location of the sun or moon in the sky. Before observatories such as Greenwich, humans used sundials — essentially a stick in the ground that casts shadows as the sun moves overhead. But this ancient link between Mother Earth and today’s clocks looks set to be severed.
Stonehenge was an ancient time-keeping system, archaeologist says
International timekeepers are on track to vote Thursday on a proposal to eliminate what’s known as a leap second — a tiny, but many say important, link between Earth’s rotation and the world’s time standard used in critical infrastructure such as telecommunications, power grids and computers.
Inserted into global clocks 27 times since 1972 , the leap second essentially allows two time systems to run in sync: astronomical time, long anchored by Earth’s rotation and measured by observatories, and Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, the global standard that’s set by ultraprecise atomic clocks first developed in the 1950s. These cutting-edge, lab-based clocks rely on tracking the natural vibrations — or ticks — of atoms.
The two time-telling methods differ because Earth does not rotate at a steady pace but wobbles, essentially making it a “lousy” clock, said Jeff Sherman, a group leader of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Time and Frequency Division in Boulder, Colorado.
This wobbling stems from various factors, such as the moon’s gravitational pull, shifts deep in the planetary core, and the movement of water and ice on Earth’s surface — an effect that’s exacerbated by the melting of the polar ice caps due to the climate crisis.
“We have to make a choice on whether or not the most important thing is a sense of time given by objects in the sky directly above, say, the Greenwich longitude,” he said referring to the Greenwich meridian that marks 0 degrees longitude. “Or you decide to follow what you believe are more stable, laboratory, man-made clocks,” Sherman added.
Leap seconds have served as the compromise between the two time-telling systems. Most people never notice them — unlike a leap year , which adds an extra day to February every four years to account for the discrepancy between the Gregorian calendar used in most parts of the world and the time it takes Earth to complete one orbit around the sun.
But the addition of leap seconds, which happens at irregular intervals and is announced with only six months’ notice, creates problems for operators of data servers, high-frequency financial trading systems and other infrastructure that rely on precise timekeeping to work properly.
The extra second crashed Reddit and LinkedIn and knocked out Qantas’ booking system in 2012. And when the most recent leap second was added at the end of 2016, customers of cloud computing provider Cloudflare briefly experienced outages or delays after its servers failed to handle the introduction of a leap second properly. Big tech players such as Meta have been calling for its demise, describing the leap second as “a major source of pain.”
The 69 member states of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, an intergovernmental organization that determines measurement standards, will meet this week in Versailles near Paris. The group, known by its French acronym BIPM, will vote on a resolution to ditch the leap second, a move that would take effect in May 2027. A majority needs to support the proposal, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the time department at BIPM.
When atomic time was first introduced, Tavella said, it was important to keep it tethered to astronomical time because navigational tools still relied on traditional celestial methods and timekeeping. With the advent of GPS, however, that was no longer the case. “This correction in time has become a serious issue for modern applications,” she added.
Why scientists say we need to send clocks to the moon — soon
Members of BIPM have discussed the switch to what Tavella called Continuous Coordinated Universal Time for more than 20 years, she noted. At the group’s last meeting in 2022, member countries voted in favor of a resolution that called for a plan to phase out the leap second on or before 2035.
In the past, some countries, such as Russia and the United Kingdom, have opposed ditching the leap second, she noted. Russia’s 2022 opposition stemmed from the fact that its Global Navigation Satellite System, or GLONASS, incorporates leap seconds, unlike other satellite navigation systems, such as the United States’ GPS and the European Union’s Galileo, that do not. The United Kingdom was once opposed because of its cultural attachment to the foundational role that Greenwich played in the history of time, but its stance has since changed, she added.
Since the world’s timekeepers last met in 2022, the debate over whether to abolish the leap second has taken on an urgency because of the prospect of something unprecedented: It will soon be necessary to subtract rather than add one second, known as a negative leap second, according to experts.
The long-term trend of Earth’s rotation is slowing, but in the near term it appears to be speeding up, potentially requiring a subtraction of a second from Coordinated Universal Time to keep astronomical and atomic time matching.
A 2025 report by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, a consortium headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, tasked with tracking Earth’s rotation, estimated that the likelihood of a negative leap second would rise sharply in the coming years — hitting a probability of 30% by 2035, according to BIPM.
Deleting a second has never previously been attempted and could create havoc in today’s digitally time-stamped world. BIPM said the operators of critical infrastructure are “largely unprepared” for such a move. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug,” the organization said, referring to Y2K, a computer flaw that programmers thought might cause severe systemic problems after December 31, 1999.
However, not everyone agrees that it’s necessary to ditch the leap second.
The technical challenges of incorporating leap seconds, whether negative or positive, into digital systems were overstated, according to Marek Ziebart, a professor of space geodesy at University College London who said there was value in keeping the world’s fundamental timescale aligned with Earth’s rotation.
“We have a system in place that uses leap seconds. It works. It maintains the timescale that all of us use on a day-to-day basis,” Ziebart said. “If you abolish the leap second, a lot of things will have to change. People will have to check their software, redesign it, fix it.”
He added that it was also “intellectually comforting” to maintain a timescale tied to Earth’s rotation. “There’s an intrinsic relationship for human beings between rotation and time,” he said. “It relates to us as animals. We’re driven by these periodicities of the sun rising, the sun setting.”
Instead of juggling positive and negative leap seconds, the BIPM resolution essentially proposes that atomic time would be allowed to drift gradually away from astronomical time. Doing so means official timekeeping would become independent of Earth’s rotation, and another leap second would never be added to clocks.
However, the proposal does recommend that the maximum difference between atomic and astronomical time should not exceed 3,600 seconds or one hour. It would take more than 3,000 years for such a difference to occur, BIPM’s Tavella said.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump , even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.
Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C. , yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud .
The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated. Malte Mueller/Getty Images hide caption
Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.
The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train .

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit .

articles.title_orig: Why a debate on declining sperm counts can spur conversations about overall health
articles.title_zh: Why a debate on declining sperm counts can spur conversations about overall health
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Jamin Brahmbhatt is a urologist and robotic surgeon with Orlando Health and an assistant professor at the University of Central Florida’s College of Medicine.
There are two times I see men get hyperfocused on their health: when they’re having issues with erections and when they’re having issues making babies.
Those with fertility concerns tend to be younger and arrive with their partners. The concerns are different, but both can open the door to a bigger conversation about health.
When an abnormal semen analysis or fertility concerns trigger a visit, I spend a lot of time sorting through things patients have heard about semen and general fertility. One fear they often mention is hearing that sperm counts are falling worldwide. Men and their partners worry less about why this is happening and more about what, if anything, they can do about it.
The more I heard this concern, the more I started to think — are sperm counts really dropping worldwide? And wait. Should I, as a man, also be worried?
Why are people talking about falling sperm counts? Alarms went off after a major global analysis published in 2022 estimated that average sperm concentration fell by about half between 1973 and 2018 among men not selected on the basis of fertility. The overall analysis combined 223 studies involving more than 57,000 men from 53 countries.
This type of research, called a meta-analysis , combines results from multiple studies to look for an overall pattern. These analyses can strongly influence how doctors and patients understand an issue and what guidance to give the general population.
Sperm counts may be declining globally, review finds, adding to debate over male fertility
Researchers estimated that average sperm concentration fell 51.6% and total sperm count fell 62.3%. Concentration measures the number of sperm per milliliter of semen, and total count measures the number in an entire ejaculate. These findings triggered alarms for researchers, doctors and patients.
When you look at the numbers, these findings do appear alarming. The numbers also raise concerns about what might be affecting sperm production. For me and others in my field, they raised another question and opportunity — could sperm measurements give a window into a man’s overall health?
I had a patient who was so stressed about dropping sperm counts that he worried about his future children and generations beyond. To him, the study sounded like a countdown to men no longer being able to reproduce. It’s a scary thought but goes beyond what the study can tell us. Other research also gives us reasons to question whether the same decline is happening everywhere.
Sperm concentration showed no overall change in the initial analysis of samples collected from 1970 through 2018, according to a 2025 review and meta-analysis . It covered 58 studies involving 11,787 American men without known infertility issues.
After adjusting for geographic region and fertility status, researchers found a modest annual decline in sperm concentration. In other words, the answer changed depending on whom was studied and how the numbers were analyzed.
These findings do not negate the concern raised by the 2022 analysis. They do make the picture more complex than a single worldwide decline. For my worried patient, that study was not a countdown clock on his chance to become a dad. I told him what I am telling you — sperm counts are fine, for now.
A doctor may commonly order a semen analysis as part of a fertility workup or after a vasectomy to ensure no sperm are left in the ejaculate. It can reveal a lot, but it cannot answer every question about fertility. The test measures several things, including how many sperm are present, how well they move and what percentage have a typical shape. The World Health Organization says its comparison numbers used to interpret the results should not be treated as an absolute line separating fertile from infertile men.
Another complicating factor is that if a man dropped off a semen sample every day for a week, the numbers would not be the same each day. Length of abstinence, recent illness, medications, stress, collection conditions and differences among labs can all affect the results. It’s why the American Urological Association recommends at least two analyses, ideally a month apart, especially when the first result may be abnormal.
I’ve seen men worry because their first test showed low motility, meaning the sperm were not moving well. I’ve also seen men with few or no sperm stay calm and simply ask, “OK, what can I do to improve this?” One test can indicate where to look. Repeated tests, interpreted alongside a medical history and examination, help make a plan.
I once treated a patient whose sperm count and shape looked fine but whose motility, or ability to move, was poor. He exercised, did not smoke and barely drank. When we talked, he opened up about work stress and poor sleep. Six months later, after improving both, his sperm movement was better. He reported no other changes to his diet or lifestyle.
Such a result does not prove better sleep and less stress caused the improvement. Semen results fluctuate. But his test results started a conversation about parts of his health that deserved attention regardless of whether his sperm improved.
Can stress affect sperm? What men should know about fertility
Most people hear sperm count and think about fertility and having kids. In my line of work, doctors see it as one part of a man’s broader health picture. Men with infertility or abnormal semen results have higher rates of some medical conditions, and urology guidelines recommend counseling them about that connection.
An abnormal semen analysis is not a diagnosis of heart disease, diabetes or an early death. It is a reason to look under the hood: Check the man’s history, examine him, review medications and consider whether another health problem is being missed.
Sperm health can be affected by some of the same conditions I discuss during a routine checkup, including medical issues, smoking, lack of sleep, heat and current medications.
Science backs me up: Obesity, diabetes and metabolic syndrome were linked with poorer semen quality and damage to sperm DNA in a review of 112 studies .
Men who slept less than six hours a night were about 40% less likely to get their partner pregnant in any given month compared with men who slept eight hours, according to a 2018 study of 1,176 couples .
Coping with ‘male menopause’: How lifestyle plays a role
Cigarette smoking can affect semen quality. In one study of infertile heavy smokers , sperm concentration and total count improved three months after they quit.
Lower sperm concentration and count were associated with exposure to heat waves in a study of men undergoing routine semen analysis in Argentina . The testicles sit outside the body for a reason. Sperm production works best below normal body temperature, and hence chronic heat exposure can interfere with that process.
What about medications such as testosterone? I tell every man who wants children now or in the future to avoid testosterone replacement therapy. Guidelines warn that it can suppress sperm production, sometimes to zero. If symptoms of low testosterone are a concern, ask about alternate options that preserve fertility.
Higher total testosterone levels were associated with GLP-1 drugs, according to a 2026 systematic review . Better semen measures in men with obesity or low testosterone have been reported in other studies.
These findings are encouraging, but I am cautious about labeling or prescribing GLP-1 drugs as fertility drugs. These medications help men lose weight and manage chronic health conditions, which may then explain the benefits seen in testosterone and sperm quality. Whether these changes improve the chances of pregnancy still needs more study.

articles.title_orig: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
articles.title_zh: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
articles.content_orig:
World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026
Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.
It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.
However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.
“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”
The International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, and promised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month .
But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.
Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, which analysts said would have little “meaningful” effect.
The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank are holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.
Launching the report in Bangkok, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said “the global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits”. She urged policymakers to “move from just coping, to rebuilding”.
Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged governments to tighten their belts , amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.
In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.
US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July – in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is poised to arrive in Bangkok later this week.
after newsletter promotion
However, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
The Fund cautioned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.
“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.
Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.
The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.
Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.
The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.
As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.

articles.title_orig: From DC to the top of the world: Taylor Knibb's Ironman triumph comes full circle
articles.title_zh: From DC to the top of the world: Taylor Knibb's Ironman triumph comes full circle
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (7News)  — Taylor Knibb has reached the pinnacle of one of the world's most grueling endurance sports. But even after winning the 2026 Ironman Triathlon World Championship, the elite athlete hasn't forgotten where her journey began — right here in the Washington, D.C. , area.
Knibb, 28, captured the world title Saturday in a dramatic finish that tested her physical limits and forced her to confront a familiar fear: what if she couldn't make it to the finish line?
The former Sidwell Friends student and Nation’s Capital Swim Club standout battled extreme fatigue, stomach issues and repeated bouts of vomiting before ultimately taking the lead late in the race and securing the championship .
In an interview with 7News Anchor Adam Longo, Knibb described a race that became as much about survival as it was about competition.
OCT 2026 - 7News' Adam Longo sits down with Taylor Knibb, a two-time Olympic silver medalist and Sidwell Friends alum, for an interview after her IRONMAN Women’s World Championship win. (7News)
"Anything can happen," she said. "Just keep moving forward and keep doing your best."
It's a philosophy that helped carry her to the world title — and one she believes applies to everyone who takes on the challenge of an Ironman, from elite professionals to first-time finishers.
An Ironman is one of the ultimate tests of endurance: competitors swim 2.4 miles, bike 112 miles and then run a full marathon of 26.2 miles. Athletes complete all three disciplines consecutively, with the clock running throughout the race.
The full-distance event can take professional athletes eight or nine hours to finish, while many amateur competitors spend well over 12 hours on the course. Athletes have a maximum of 17 hours to complete the race under standard Ironman rules.
For Knibb, the final miles of this year's championship became a test of just how much she could endure.
With roughly 12 kilometers — about 7.5 miles — remaining in the marathon , Knibb decided she needed to slow down at an aid station to take care of herself.
"I was like, wow, like it was really getting hard and hot," she recalled. "You need to take care of yourself so you don't — so last year doesn't happen again."
Knibb was leading last year's race with two miles to go before she collapsed and was unable to continue, resulting in a DNF.
She walked through the aid station, taking time to get what she needed before returning to the course. But she began vomiting as she ran away from the station.
When rival Solveig Lovseth passed her, Knibb faced a difficult decision: push harder to stay in contention or protect herself from another devastating collapse.
Rather than fixating on the title slipping away, Knibb focused on what she could control.
"Making it to the finish line is a tremendous accomplishment and a huge win," she said.
Then, with roughly two kilometers — about 1.2 miles — remaining, the race took another unexpected turn. Knibb learned that Lovseth was down on the course.
She passed her rival but was still struggling herself, vomiting again as she made her way down a major descent toward the finish.
The moment was complicated by the reality of competing in an extreme endurance event: Knibb knew what it felt like to push her body to its limits, and she understood the danger of what her competitor was experiencing.
"It's really scary," Knibb said. "As competitors, we respect each other, and you just don't want to see your competitor in that kind of position because it's dangerous."
Despite her own physical distress, Knibb kept moving forward — and crossed the finish line as world champion.
The lessons of last year's heartbreak
Knibb's determination to finish this year's race was shaped in part by the disappointment of the previous championship event.
She said avoiding a repeat of last year's collapse became a central focus as the race unfolded.
"I was most scared of myself imploding again because I didn't want a repeat of that," she said.
The experience changed how she measured success. Winning the championship mattered, but so did making smart decisions, listening to her body and getting across the finish line safely.
That approach ultimately put her in position to win.
For Knibb, the result reinforced one of the sport's defining lessons: success doesn't always follow a straight line, and even the world's best athletes have to adapt when things go wrong.
A champion shaped by the D.C. area
Long before she became an Ironman world champion, Knibb was a young athlete developing her talents in the Washington region.
She attended Sidwell Friends School and swam with Nation’s Capital Swim Club, an experience she credits with helping lay the foundation for her career.
Knibb said her swim coach recognized early on that her passion extended beyond the pool and into triathlon. Rather than forcing her to choose one path, he supported her ambitions across multiple disciplines.
"He could see that my love was really with triathlon and the swim was a piece of that," Knibb said.
She remembers the club as an environment that encouraged athletes to develop not only their competitive abilities but also their interests and identities beyond a single sport.
"I think that environment for a swim club that can produce such amazing swimmers, but also be able to see the other side in terms of developing other athletes and other humans — I think that was really special, really important to me," she said.
"That was a huge foundation of everything and everything I've learned and the person I am."
A family moment years in the making
One of the most emotional moments of the championship came after Knibb crossed the finish line and embraced her mother Leslie.
Knibb said having her mother there made the victory especially meaningful. The previous year's race had presented a different circumstance, and she noted that her mother would not have been at the finish had she won because she was competing in the event herself.
"It was so special, and I couldn't have scripted it better," Knibb said.
She described her mother as someone who leads by example rather than pressuring her to pursue a particular sport or career.
"She's never told me I have to do triathlon," Knibb said. "She's never told me that I have to do anything."
The embrace was a reminder that behind the hours of training and the international accolades is a family that has supported her journey.
Before Taylor became a champion, there was Leslie
Taylor Knibb didn't discover triathlon by accident. She grew up watching her mother compete in endurance races, absorbing the sport's culture long before she became a world champion herself.
Leslie began racing in the early 1990s and built an impressive résumé of her own, including multiple Ironman finishes and top age-group performances at the Ironman World Championships. In 2010, when Taylor was 12, she traveled to Kona, Hawaii, to watch her mother finish 11th in her age group — a memory that would help fuel her own ambition to one day race on that same world stage.
Leslie's influence extended well beyond the race course. A longtime member of the D.C. Triathlon Club, she became a coach in 2012, working with adult beginners and young elite and junior athletes in the Washington area. She also supported local paratriathletes through USA Triathlon's Mid-Atlantic paratriathlon committee, helping develop opportunities for athletes with disabilities. Her involvement reflects the community-oriented side of triathlon — helping newcomers find their footing in a sport that can seem intimidating to outsiders.
Despite her daughter's extraordinary success, Leslie has been careful to let Taylor chart her own course. Taylor has said her mother never pressured her to pursue triathlon, and Leslie has emphasized the importance of allowing her children to find their own passions. That approach helped turn childhood curiosity into an Olympic career and, ultimately, a world championship.

articles.title_orig: Champ 8s: Deep Field Includes Dutch M8, US W4 World Champs and WR Holders, Defending Champs, Tokyo NZ M8, More
articles.title_zh: Champ 8s: Deep Field Includes Dutch M8, US W4 World Champs and WR Holders, Defending Champs, Tokyo NZ M8, More
articles.content_orig:
HOCR Race Director Brendan Mulvey called both the men's and women's Champ Eights fields "deeper than they've been in recent years," and there is much to look forward to late Sunday afternoon when the big boats take to the water.
In the women's field, USRowing will defend its championship with a boat that includes everyone from the gold-medal four at last August's World Championships. It'll also be Thames-on-the-Charles in the Women's race, with boats from Molesey, Leander, Tyrian, and Thames Rowing all entered, in addition to crews from Oxford and Cambridge maybe providing a preview of next spring's Boat Race. And Yale, Brown, Radcliffe and Princeton will lead a full complement of American colleges.
On the men's side Cambridge University will be looking to not only defend its title, but win its third in a row, something that hasn't been done in the Champ Eights since USRowing won nine in a row from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. Chasing Cambridge up the course will be Washington and Harvard, two and three seconds behind the Light Blue one year ago, and looking to snap championship droughts that go back five years in Washington's case, fifteen in Harvard's.
A reunion boat of New Zealand's gold medalists from the Tokyo Olympics will lead an international contingent that includes boats from Ireland, France, the Netherlands and Canada. And, like the women, the men's race will have its own Boat Race preview as boats from Oxford join their ancient rival in the field.
But the boat creating all the pre-Regatta buzz is the Holland Acht, filled to the brim with two-time and reigning World Champions. The Dutch will have nine world champions in their boat, bringing eight of the nine gold medalists from Amsterdam this past August, and filling the empty seat with Eli Brouwer, the bowman from their 2025 world championship boat in Shanghai.
The Dutch athletes are still on a high from their win in front of home country fans. "Winning once is very hard; winning twice is so much harder," said Jonna de Vries, the Dutch coxswain. "To do it in front of our home fans, it was just fabulous."
Like most rowers and crews after a successful Olympics or World Championships, the Dutch have been on holiday for much of the fall, staying away from the boat for a full three weeks in September. But before they broke, they marked the Head of the Charles as the Regatta where they would get back to work. They know they're coming to Boston with a bullseye on their bow, and they're fine with that. "It's really fun, really cool to be the ones everyone wants to beat," de Vries said. They have rowing the eight for the last two weeks, and, according to de Vries, training very hard and training well.
De Vries has coxed in the Head of the Charles before, back in 2013-2014, and, like so many athletes, has warm memories of the experience. "I just remember it being so iconic, the leaves and the crowds and the bridges and the noise," she said. "It's really a special event." What she remembers from the course from her earlier visits is that she had a boat with "a good rudder," and was able to steer a clean course.
She's excited about coming back because she knows it's a course when a coxswain can make a big difference. "I love head racing. It's fun, it's a challenge, and you can really show what you mean to the boat."
As to all the boats looking to take down the world champions, de Vries voiced a particular respect for USRowing. "They start behind us, and that's good because the boys can see them." The Dutch start at bow four, the Americans at six.
She also expects a strong race from Cambridge. "We share a coach," she said, "so we have some intel, and we know they're rowing very well." But the Dutch may have gotten something of a surprise psychological advantage over the defending champions. Holland Acht will be rowing a shell borrowed from Harvard, and it just happens to be the shell that Cambridge rowed in their two victories. "We know they want to win the triple," de Vries said. "But we're telling them it will be the boat that gets the triple."
