articles.title_orig: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? | Sean Ingle
articles.title_zh: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? | Sean Ingle
articles.content_orig:
Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act
W hen Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing . “Bring it on Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!”
That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2hr 9min 56sec, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1min 57sec, but her personal best by a staggering five minutes. Afterwards she was asked by Robert Johnson of Let’s Run what her response was to those who believed she must be doping. “People must talk,” she replied. “I don’t know.”
We know a lot more now. Because five months after that epic run, Chepngetich’s star came crashing down to earth. First she failed a doping test. Then she was banned for three years . These days people in the sport talk about her reluctantly, like a family member who has joined a mysterious cult. Yet her world record still stands because she passed a test after the race itself.
What should we think of this? What are we allowed legally to say about this? And what, if anything, can be done about it?
A couple of weeks ago, I spoke to Brett Clothier, the head of the Athletics Integrity Unit, which prosecuted the case against Chepngetich, to ask about her world record. “It is not satisfactory, to be frank,” he admitted. “But the world anti-doping code is pretty clearcut on the rights athletes have, even if they’re found guilty of a doping offence.”
That much is true. But while legally Chepngetich was clean when she broke her world record, the fact it stands surely damages the sport’s credibility.
True, there are plenty of highly suspicious records from the 80s and early 90s, given what we know about state-sponsored doping behind the iron curtain and in China. And if you believe Florence Griffith Joyner knocked more than half a second off her 100m and 200m times in 1988 by doing 5,000 sit-ups a day and drinking water, I have some magic beans to sell you.
Griffith Joyner, of course, never tested positive. But before her death aged 38, her fellow American sprinter Darrell Robinson claimed in a paid interview with the German magazine Stern that he had sold her human growth hormone for $2,000.
He also alleged that she had told him : “If you want to make a million dollars, you’ve got to invest a couple of thousand.” Yet as much as Flo-Jo’s records make us uneasy, they are seen as coming from a bygone and more lawless era.
Also, what makes Chepngetich unique is that no other athlete has been hit with a lengthy ban so soon after a world record.
The Kenyan’s defence for being 20 times the legal limit of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) in her system? That she had taken her housemaid’s medication after feeling hot and having a rapid resting heartbeat. It was, the AIU noted, a “hardly credible” explanation .
The AIU also found screenshots on Chepngetich’s phone about the banned drug testosterone and “messages related to unidentified third parties working on ‘programs’ possibly related to doping”. The Kenyan has insisted that she has never used testosterone and the messages were from a group chat, but they hardly inspire confidence either.
So what can be done? The short answer, having spoken to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), is very little. As a Wada spokesperson pointed out to me, removing her results before her positive test “in the absence of any evidence or reasonable inference that the athlete was doping before or at the time of the earlier results, might well breach a number of legal principles including proportionality and human rights.”
after newsletter promotion
But what about Lance Armstrong, who was stripped of his Tour de France titles despite not being convicted of breaking any doping rules while competing? Could this not apply here? Not according to Wada.
“He had procedural avenues open to him to contest the sanction but ultimately chose not to use them,” a spokesperson told me. “That makes his case a relatively weak precedent for establishing how far retrospective disqualification could legally go.”
One idea I floated to various experts was the idea that athletes could be asked to sign a social contract, which pledged they would accept losing their world record if they tested positive within a year of that world record or winning an Olympic medal.
In theory, one anti-doping expert put it to me, it was possible to do this. But he felt it would require everybody – from sports federations and governments to athlete bodies and human rights groups – to buy in and to agree to change the Wada code to allow retrospective punishments. And that is not going to happen.
At least track and field can point to many significant victories over doping in the last decade, given that Chepngetich is one of 317 elite Kenyan athletes the AIU has caught since it was set up in 2017. Many sports pay lip service to catching cheats. Athletics actually does. And the AIU does it on a modest budget of $11.9m (£9m) a year.
There are also positive signs that prominent athletes realise more must be done when it comes to anti-doping. Before Sabastian Sawe set his men’s marathon world record in London, for instance, his sponsors, Adidas, paid $50,000 for extra testing. Nike did the same for two of their athletes, Jacob Kiplimo and Brigid Kosgei, before Chicago.
Sawe’s agent, Eric Lilot, wants to go further by making his athletes sign a contract that will require them to give up any money still owed to them if it is shown they intentionally tried to dope. All that points to brighter days ahead, however much Chepngetich’s record makes us feel queasy.

articles.title_orig: Why an ageing world is a question for young people
articles.title_zh: Why an ageing world is a question for young people
articles.content_orig:
By XANTHA LEATHAM, EXECUTIVE SCIENCE EDITOR
Published: 11:32 EDT, 12 October 2026 | Updated: 11:32 EDT, 12 October 2026
For many young people, few things are more alarming than seeing their phone light up with an unexpected call.
Now, experts have revealed Gen Z would rather do almost anything than pick up the phone – because surprise conversations trigger anxiety.
Sophie Riegel, a best-selling author who specialises in intergenerational relationships, said people aged between 14 and 29 see an unscheduled call as a demand for their immediate attention.
Chatting on the phone is often seen as stressful, awkward and emotionally demanding, she revealed.
The expert admits to avoiding calls herself, explaining it requires a ‘live performance’ and is an ‘inefficient’ use of time.
‘A call to say hi or ask a simple question causes unnecessary anxiety, which is why we prefer a text,’ she wrote in a post on Psychology Today .
Instead, she argued that older generations should text younger people first to let them know they are about to ring.
Experts have revealed Gen Z would rather do almost anything than pick up the phone - because surprise conversations trigger anxiety
In her piece, Ms Riegel cites a 2024 study that found a quarter of 18-to-34-year-olds never answer calls and 70 per cent prefer texts.
The same study also revealed that more than half of young adults associate unexpected calls with bad news.
She explained that receiving a text allows a person to wait until they are ready to respond.
‘A phone call requires my attention right here, right now,’ she said. ‘Because I don’t work a typical 9-to-5, people often assume I’m free at any hour.
‘When the phone rings in the middle of a focused work block, answering means dropping everything and rebuilding my concentration later.’
She also argued that picking up the phone means being ‘on’.
‘I have to answer in real time, with no chance to pause and choose my words,’ she said. ‘Texting gives me a safety net (and a backspace button).
‘Calls also come with small talk I didn’t sign up for and an uncomfortable goodbye that takes three attempts to complete. It’s all doable, but it is draining.’
Ms Riegel added that speaking on the phone can feel inefficient, with a quick question easily ending in a 20-minute conversation.
‘While I enjoy catching up, I’d rather do it when I can give the conversation my full attention,’ she wrote.
‘For a quick question, a text gets the answer across in seconds and leaves a record I can scroll back to.’
A phone call can also trigger anxiety, she explained, with surprise phone calls ‘sending alarm bells ringing’.
To tackle the issue, Ms Riegel suggests a compromise between the two generations.
She advises that Gen Z pick up the phone when they are free, but that older people do not take it personally if someone is not able to answer.
The best thing to do, she says, is text first. ‘A quick “Free to call tonight?” removes the alarm of an unexpected call and lets us pick a time when I can give you my full attention,’ she wrote.
‘If you have a question that requires a short answer, a text works. If you want to catch up or have an emotional conversation, a call is better.’
Finally, she recommends saving surprise calls for urgent moments.
‘That way, when my phone rings unexpectedly, I know it’s important, and I’ll answer,’ she added.
Whether you’re a Gen Z terrified of picking up the phone or simply feeling disconnected compared to easier times when dialling a number instead of texting a one-word response felt normal - don’t panic! Follow these simple steps to help you make the perfect phone call…
1) Making the first move and calling a person can feel daunting - to boost your confidence ahead of the big moment, try making a list of points you want to cover first.
2) First impressions count, so instead of mumbling a ‘hello’ at the start the call, greet the other person and introduce yourself in a bright tone - even if they know who you are.
3) Own the call, don’t let the call own you. With no visual cues it can be hard to know when to speak – but if you set out the agenda for the conversation, you can lead the call and chat with confidence.
4) Make the call your core focus. It can be tempting to move around and multitask while on the phone, but if you sit and only focus on the call it will help you actively listen to the other person and form a stronger bond.
5) At the end of the call, summarise the conversation to ensure you are both on the same page to eliminate any anxiety.
6) And of course when the call ends, remind the other person that they can simply pick up the phone instead of texting you next time!

articles.title_orig: Who are the Houthis in Yemen and what do they want?
articles.title_zh: Who are the Houthis in Yemen and what do they want?
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months, with fierce fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi movement, which controls much of the country's north-west, and Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
In September, the Houthis seized part of Yemen's Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Their advance contributed to a further rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
At the start of October, pro-government forces said they had managed to regain control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of intense Saudi air strikes.
The Houthis responded to the strikes by launching missiles and drones at military bases, energy facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia. At least 13 people were killed when a missile hit Riyadh's international airport on 10 October - the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.
They are an armed political and religious group from northern Yemen which champions the country's Zaidi minority. Zaidism is a branch of Shia Islam.
The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed groups such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.
Formally known as Ansar Allah (Partisans of God), the group emerged in the 1990s and takes its name from the movement's late founder, Hussein al-Houthi. His brother, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has been its de facto leader since 2004.
In the early 2000s, the Houthis fought several rebellions against Yemen's long-time authoritarian president Ali Abdullah Saleh. They wanted greater autonomy for the group's homeland in the north of Yemen.
During the 2011 Arab Spring, a popular uprising forced Saleh to hand over power to his deputy, Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.
President Hadi's government was overwhelmed with problems and the Houthis seized control of the northern province of Saada before capturing the capital Sanaa in 2014.
In 2015, they seized large parts of western Yemen and forced Hadi to flee abroad, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene on behalf of the government.
The fighting since then has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
The Houthis have continued to grow in strength, with UN experts estimating they had recruited up to 350,000 fighters by 2024. They control between one-quarter and one-third of Yemen's territory, where about three-quarters of the population live.
Saudi Arabia feared the Houthis would take over Yemen and make it a satellite of the kingdom's regional rival, Iran, when they ousted the government from Sanaa.
The Saudis formed a coalition with other Arab states that began an air campaign in 2015 aimed at restoring the government's authority. They received logistical and intelligence support from the US, UK and France.
But years of air strikes and fighting on the ground by the Yemeni military and anti-Houthi militias were unable to dislodge the Houthis from most of the territory they seized.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 that largely halted the fighting. That year also saw Hadi transfer his powers to a new Presidential Leadership Council, which oversees the Aden-based government.
Soon after the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, the Houthis began firing drones and missiles towards Israel and at merchant vessels in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying they were acting in support of the Palestinians.
Western countries deployed warships to protect shipping, and the US, UK and Israel carried out air strikes intended to degrade the Houthis' military capabilities. Israeli strikes also killed senior Houthi figures, including the prime minister of the group's self-declared government.
The Houthis paused attacks on Israel after the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza but resumed them after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026.
The informal ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudis began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they called the Saudi "blockade" of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that month which they blamed on Saudi Arabia.
This was followed by a rapid Houthi advance in September that captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coastline, including the port city of Mokha and the island of Perim (Mayyun).
The move gave the Houthis significant control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, but they insisted that they posed no threat to international shipping, except for Saudi-linked vessels.
In October, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Since then, pro-government forces have reportedly regained control of areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes. But the Houthis have denied losing territory there.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on the ground in Yemen during the escalation. The UN says more than 200,000 people have been newly displaced.
The Houthis' actions have caused renewed concern about disruption of world oil supplies. Bab al-Mandab became an important route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia after shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, was curtailed due to the US and Israel's war with Iran.
The situation has also been exacerbated by Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and oil and gas facilities, as well as an attack in September on the kingdom's East-West Pipeline that was blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
The escalation has threatened to again draw in Western powers.
Following the deadly attack on Riyadh airport, US President Trump said he was going to "make a decision" about whether the US would join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
The UK meanwhile agreed in September to deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi fighter jets in mid-air for "purely defensive missions".
Saudi Arabia and Western powers say Iran smuggled weapons - including drones, and cruise and ballistic missiles - to the Houthis during Yemen's civil war in violation of a UN arms embargo.
A panel of UN experts concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of material, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Lebanon's Hezbollah movement and Iraqi specialists.
And a report in May 2026 by Conflict Armament Research (CAR) - after the start of the Iran war - found that whereas in the past Tehran shipped finished weapons to the Houthis, it was now increasingly sending parts which its proxies were able to assemble and was also sharing increasingly advanced missile technologies.
Iran has denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.

articles.title_orig: World Bank President: AI infrastructure boom shows no signs of slowing
articles.title_zh: World Bank President: AI infrastructure boom shows no signs of slowing
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.
"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."
Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.
What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.
That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.
The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.
World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."
The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.
Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday.
AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.
Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

articles.title_orig: EU Plans Limits on Chinese Hybrid Car Imports
articles.title_zh: EU Plans Limits on Chinese Hybrid Car Imports
articles.content_orig:
Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
Business live – latest updates
VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry
The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week .
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.
Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.
Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.
On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
after newsletter promotion
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.
Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.
“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Sacramento teen competes for Team USA at World Skate Games in Paraguay
articles.title_zh: Sacramento teen competes for Team USA at World Skate Games in Paraguay
articles.content_orig:
Axel Moore, a 17-year-old speedskater from Sacramento, is representing Team USA in the Junior division at the World Skate Games in Paraguay
Axel Moore, a 17-year-old speedskater from Sacramento, is representing Team USA in the Junior division at the World Skate Games in Paraguay
Seventeen-year-old Axel Moore from Sacramento is representing Team USA this week at the World Skate Games in Paraguay, competing against top athletes from around the globe.
“Basically, every roller sport we have from skateboarding, downhill skating, speed skating, and artistic skating [is] coming together in Asunción, Paraguay, this year to all compete at the same place at the same time,” said Moore, who will compete in the Junior Division.
Last year, Moore was unable to compete for Team USA due to the cost of traveling to the competition in China. This year, with the help of a GoFundMe campaign, he gets to wear the USA uniform.
“I’m super proud to represent my country in Paraguay,” Moore said. “It feels like a chance to get back from last year that I didn’t get to go.”
Moore’s journey into the sport began unexpectedly during a family outing.
“Every Saturday when I was a kid, me and my dad and my sister used to go out, and we called it Dad-er day,” laughed Moore. “And one of the Saturdays, he was like, ‘We go skating, guys.’ And I said, ‘No, no, we don’t want to go.’ And he finally wore us down, convinced us. We went. And then I said, ‘Let’s go next week, too.’ And then I was pretty much every week after that for the next ten years.”
What started as a fun weekly event turned into serious training. Moore then joined Triad Racing.
“It’s special to see him come in from a nine-year-old kid to, you know, almost a man and be able to go and represent the country and represent us,” said Josh Jozwiak, Triad Racing’s head coach.
Moore, now a three-time indoor national champion, is focused on giving this competition everything he's got.
“I try to minimize stress. Mostly I want to remain as calm as possible before I get out there. And I just want to stay ready and stay warm,” Moore said.
“Our focus is on looking at what we can control, not worrying about whoever else is out there,” Jozwiak said. “At the end of the day, to me, his best effort is the result that matters, not the end result of ending on that podium.”
Jozwiak can feel that way because of everything that Moore has already given to the sport and to him as a coach.
“He has invested a ton in the local athletes in this area that compete in this sport,” Jozwiak said. “He will leave behind a legacy that he may never even realize, because he has affected people’s lives in ways that they may never tell him. And that’s a pretty cool thing to leave behind when you do walk away from the sport.”
The World Skate Games take place over a two-week period, and Moore’s final race is scheduled for this Saturday, October 17th, in the 100-meter race.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he’s ‘looking at’ firing Kimberly Guilfoyle from Athens post
articles.title_zh: Trump says he’s ‘looking at’ firing Kimberly Guilfoyle from Athens post
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is weighing firing the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of her alleged improper behaviour in Athens, which she has denied.
Asked if he was considering sacking her, Trump told reporters at the White House: "We're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy." She is the ex-fiancée of the president's son, Donald Trump Jr.
The Wall Street Journal reported Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration.
Her lawyers denied any wrongdoing by Guilfoyle and said she was owed the money for speaking engagements and consulting work for the donor.
Guilfoyle, 57, a former Fox News host and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was appointed as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
At the time, Trump said "her extensive experience and leadership in law, media and politics, along with her sharp intellect make her supremely qualified" to represent the US abroad.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by the Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Deters never sent the money. Guilfoyle's lawyers have disputed the authenticity of the messages.
They said in a two-page statement on 12 October that Deters owed Guilfoyle about $150,000 for speeches and consulting work that she performed for him long before her ambassadorship.
"Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption," they said.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle boasting of her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees have been calling on the state department to investigate her conduct in Greece.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured with Guilfoyle last week during his trip to Athens, was also reported to be unhappy with her in light of the allegations.
A former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, she joined Fox News in 2006.
After leaving broadcasting in 2018, she joined the Trump campaign. The same year, she began a relationship with Donald Jr, and the couple eventually became engaged.
The pair reportedly parted ways in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.
Donald Jr wed socialite and model Bettina Anderson last year in Florida.

articles.title_orig: U.S. and NATO commander vows to thwart Moscow, warns Kyiv over refinery strikes
articles.title_zh: U.S. and NATO commander vows to thwart Moscow, warns Kyiv over refinery strikes
articles.content_orig:
Professor Azeem Ibrahim says Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic enclave has become a testing ground for hybrid warfare targeting European infrastructure.
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that what he called the "lethal alliance" would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault.
"Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland , in an apparent warning to Moscow.
"This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force," he said during a panel titled "Theory of Victory: How Do We Achieve Military Success Against Russia in Deterrence and Defence?" on the first day of the forum.
US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that the alliance would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe, also outlined a three-pronged strategy of "blocking, blunting and breaking" enemy forces, making clear that while NATO is a defensive alliance, it is prepared to respond decisively to an assault on any of its 32 members.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile."
The warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow.
"We stand here together in Poland today stronger than ever united in our common vision of a more balanced, more ready and more lethal alliance," Grynkewich also said.
European officials have accused Russia of waging a campaign of hybrid warfare involving sabotage, arson and cyberattacks, alongside increasingly provocative military activity near NATO territory.
I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA
Grynkewich's warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
In 2025, multiple Russian drones entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on Ukraine, prompting a response from Polish and allied aircraft.
NATO launched Operation Eastern Sentry to strengthen defenses along its eastern flank.
Romania has also reported Russian drone incursions , while Estonia has accused Russian military aircraft of violating its airspace.
Grynkewich's remarks had followed a tense weekend between Russia and Ukraine, with Moscow launching fresh strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite diplomatic efforts to reduce hostilities.
President Donald Trump had announced that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the U.S. and global markets.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania. ( Photo by Contributor/Getty Images)
The reported agreement included a waiver of certain U.S. sanctions on Russian energy exports.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, casting doubt on prospects for a broader ceasefire.
The tensions have also been accompanied by recent nuclear warnings from Moscow.
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad , its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic note obtained by Reuters , Moscow accused NATO of pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" that carried "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
According to the note, Russia warned it could use its full military arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend Kaliningrad and raised the possibility of strikes against decision-making centers in NATO countries at the outset of a conflict.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte rejected the threats, emphasizing the alliance's defensive mission and calling on Moscow to end its war in Ukraine.
"Putin knows that he can never win from NATO," Rutte said during a Sept. 30 appearance at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit .
Putin has also maintained that Russia has no plans to attack European countries and wants peaceful coexistence with its neighbors.
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name during his Warsaw address, but his warning appeared directed at Moscow and with NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept also identifying Russia as the most significant and direct threat to allied security.
"My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance," Grynkewich said on Monday.
"And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us."
Grynkewich said NATO was already putting the strategy into action through military exercises, enhanced military readiness and investments in new capabilities.

The general made clear that NATO's response would not necessarily be limited to enemy troops directly involved in an assault, but could extend to the broader military infrastructure enabling the attack.
Meanwhile, Trump has pressed European allies to increase defense spending and has questioned whether countries that fail to meet their obligations should expect U.S. protection.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment, recalling Trump's positive remarks about the alliance during the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands.
"I was in the room and I felt the love," Grynkewich said of the 2025 event.
"What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we've got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he added.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Airport Attacks Pressure Trump to Boost US Role in Yemen
articles.title_zh: Saudi Airport Attacks Pressure Trump to Boost US Role in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Houthi missile attack on Riyadh airport: Saudi Arabia vows resilience
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days.
In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest.
All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said.
Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat.
The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”.
The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11.
Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities.
The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience.
“The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”.
Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on.
One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh.
US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group.
A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency.
Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.
The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23.

articles.title_orig: Poland: Germany detains 2 in connection with Starlink fire
articles.title_zh: Poland: Germany detains 2 in connection with Starlink fire
articles.content_orig:
Polish officials on Monday said that two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany in connection with a fire last month at a Starlink station in Poland .
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is widely used by the military of Poland's neighbor Ukraine amid the Russian invasion .
Officials from several EU countries have been warning of mounting Russian sabotage, cyber and hybrid attacks across Europe aiming either to erode support for Ukraine or to impact Ukraine directly.
Polish officials did not specify exactly where or when the two men were allegedly detained in Germany.
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported the arrests on Monday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk following soon after.
"On behalf of Polish services, German police detained two Turkish citizens suspected of setting fire to a Starlink station in Masovia," he said on social media. "This is another act of hybrid warfare. The perpetrators of the sabotage will answer before the Polish justice system."
Masovia is the province that includes the Polish capital Warsaw, not that far from Poland's eastern borders to Belarus and Ukraine.
Poland's Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak alleged that Russia was behind the incident.
He also told a press conference that, "​it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld" for such attacks.
Russia typically dismisses European claims of hybrid warfare or systemic sabotage as either anti-Russian hysteria or disinformation.

articles.title_orig: A generation of angry young Indians takes to the streets to challenge Modi
articles.title_zh: A generation of angry young Indians takes to the streets to challenge Modi
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a " mother of democracy ," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying.
"A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms.
Earlier today, key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission .
CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests.
On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission.
Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports.
Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government .
"There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend.
"Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy ," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi.
Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists.
The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments.
Experts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest.
"If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC.
He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it.
The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled."
On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India."
The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations.
The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2 , seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters.
On Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls . It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list ."
However, Modi's ruling party, the Bharatiya Janata Party, has defended the Election Commission and said the deletions were made on account of 28 million people who died, 68 million who relocated, 10 million with duplicate entries and 30 million absent or non-traceable voters.
The sweeping revisions of the electoral roll have raised serious constitutional and legal questions, Milan Vaishnav, director and senior fellow of the South Asia Program at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told CNBC.
The core demand of the movement is for Kumar to resign and for the commission to "seriously modify the so-called 'Special Intensive Revision' of the electoral rolls," he said.

articles.title_orig: Asia stocks slide as China chip threat hits Samsung, SK Hynix; oil retreats
articles.title_zh: Asia stocks slide as China chip threat hits Samsung, SK Hynix; oil retreats
articles.content_orig:
Technology stocks fell Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition.
Micron was down around 3% in U.S. premarket trading, with other names like Broadcom under pressure.
European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open.
Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August.
In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.
Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%.
The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure.
Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space.
"Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling.
"In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email.
CXMT shares were down over 2%.
Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected.
But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share.
"More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said.
He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape.
"I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power.
The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.

articles.title_orig: IMF warns bond yields could see a 'disorderly' spike as debt, inflation risks worsen
articles.title_zh: IMF warns bond yields could see a 'disorderly' spike as debt, inflation risks worsen
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK – The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets.
Government bond yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation.
In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that sovereign bond risk could deteriorate, warning of "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The report was released Tuesday as part of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, this week, where more than 18,000 delegates gathered to discuss the state of the world economy and the financial system.
High debt load and rollover risks make the bond market "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," the report said. The IMF had warned last week that global public debt had reached near its highest level since World War II and was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP.
"Impact could be severe given the foundational importance of sovereign bond markets," the IMF said Tuesday. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral.
IMF also noted the exponentially rising borrowing by AI firms — that compete with sovereign bonds for investor demand — as an additional source of strain on bond markets. Hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance has risen to 10% from less than 1% since 2024, the report said.
The global AI buildout has seen tech giants, such as Alphabet Inc's Google, Meta Platforms , hyperscalers and AI labs raising hundreds of billions of dollars in debt this year.
"AI-linked issuance – much of it longer-dated – has grown large enough to compete with government bonds for investor capital, even if it does not appear to be the dominant driver of yields," according to Marc Seidner, CIO of non-traditional strategies at Pacific Investment Management.
Hedge funds' growing holdings of Treasuries leave the market "susceptible to a disorderly unwind," the IMF said. Leveraged basis trades have partly unwound without notable pressure in the short-term loan market but the leverage that remains is a concern.
Hedge funds' share of U.S. Treasuries rose to about 9% in 2025 from about 4% in 2022, mostly through highly arbitraged strategies, the IMF said, citing data from the Federal Reserve.
Caio Ferreira, IMF deputy division chief for financial supervision and regulation, said the worry stems from hedge funds' rising leverage and their increasingly overlapping positions, meaning multiple funds are holding the same trades, potentially amplifying impact from a collective unwinding.
On the bright side, liquidity has held up in the U.S., Europe and the U.K., the IMF said. Japan is the exception: liquidity in its government bond market has "continued to deteriorate" as yield volatility has risen since the end of yield curve control.
The fund urged debt managers to lengthen maturities, warning that rollover risk could be exacerbated by strategies that replace long-term debt with short-term borrowing on a large scale.
The IMF sounded the alarm over a web of "circular" financing deals among AI firms.
Since 2023, 14 publicly disclosed deals channeled about $300 billion of equity, led by hyperscalers, into financially weaker AI firms, alongside $650 billion of debt. In exchange, the investors secured $1.4 trillion of "future revenue commitments" through services or chip orders, the IMF said.
The revenue promises are what set the deals apart, Jason Wu, assistant director of the IMF monetary and capital markets department, said at a press briefing on Tuesday. "What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments, hence the circularity."
If AI commercialization falls short, the losses could arrive together. "If there are questions about the monetization in AI, the equity investments will deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service, and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialize," Wu said, describing what he called a "triple whammy."
Such heavy financing and revenue promises cluster in a handful of AI firms, the report said. Due to that concentration, "there are certain companies and nodes that are particularly exposed," Wu said. "If there are some kind of issues with those entities, then the circularity would pose risk to the market."

articles.title_orig: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
articles.title_zh: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
articles.content_orig:
High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks
IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”
An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.
It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.
The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.
Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.
The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.
Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.
The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.
The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.
after newsletter promotion
In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.
In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.
It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals , tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.
It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.
In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.
He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.
“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience.
“The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”.
Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on.
One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh.
US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group.
A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency.
Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.
The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23.

articles.title_orig: Samsung, SK Hynix shares plunge on China competition fears
articles.title_zh: Samsung, SK Hynix shares plunge on China competition fears
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment.
Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.9% — both hit their lowest intra-day levels since August.
In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.03%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.
Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.6%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.38%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.76%, Disco lost 4.83% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.89%.
The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure.
Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space.
"Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling.
"In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email.
CXMT shares were down over 2%.
Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected.
But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share.
"More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said.
He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape.
"I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power.
The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.

articles.title_orig: El Nino Watch: the impacts around the world this week
articles.title_zh: El Nino Watch: the impacts around the world this week
articles.content_orig:
Food security concerns, wildfires and power warnings are among the impacts around the world this week from an exceptionally strong El Nino weather cycle.
Here is a look at how this year's phenomenon, in which a warmer sea surface shifts global weather patterns, has been affecting people globally:
El Nino is associated with strong drought in Indonesia, where tracts of forest and plantations have been burning in biodiverse Borneo and the South Sumatra region for months.
The fires have caused a regional haze crisis, with Malaysia last week closing schools in several regions and Singapore announcing subsidies for people seeking medical treatment for haze-linked illness.
Malaysia has called for a meeting of regional body ASEAN to discuss the haze, and offered firefighting assistance.
Experts say years of deforestation and peatland drainage in Indonesia have made it more vulnerable to fires during dry periods.
The fires have sickened tens of thousands of people, while conservationists have rescued dozens of orangutans trapped by smoke and flames, including Novita, a female found clinging to a treetop with burns on her hands and feet.
"She had to leave her habitat, and we had to rescue her, primarily because of the flames," said Andi Muhammad Khadafi, head of the Central Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency.
Haze from fires also blanketed Manaus, the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon, where public schools were shut on Friday.
Amazonas state recorded nearly four times more fire hotspots this September than the year before. On Wednesday alone, over 749 fires were burning.
Myanmar warned citizens to expect power outages as the electricity grid is strained by an unseasonal heatwave authorities blamed on El Nino.
"Due to the effects of severe El Nino conditions, temperatures across the country have risen significantly, resulting in increased electricity consumption," the energy ministry said.
Weather officials also warned the country to expect "abnormal" rainfall, drought, extreme heat and drinking water shortages.
In the Philippines, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the government was preparing for higher demand and the possibility of hydropower declines due to hotter and drier weather.
"The appeal is for the public to be aware of this so that we can all start having the mindset of energy savings," she said.
International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva told AFP she is "very concerned" about El Nino's global impacts, particularly on food security.
The IMF is "getting ready" to offer support to countries that may struggle to absorb the impact, she added.
The United Nations Development Programme also warned Sunday that the combined impacts of higher borrowing costs, surging energy prices and the powerful El Nino created "a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty".
In southern Madagascar, aid workers told AFP they are already battling the effects of a famine and conditions are expected to worsen as El Nino's full impact on Africa takes hold from this month.
El Nino will continue intensifying until a December peak, the UN's World Meteorological Organization said Thursday.
"It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions," the body said in its monthly update.
Sea-surface temperatures in a key monitoring region in the Pacific reached an "all-time high" last month, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service said, while Japan's weather agency on Friday declared this El Nino was of "the strongest intensity on record".
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino, and the comparison is complicated by the background effects of climate change.
29.70C: the all-time high sea-surface temperature recorded in part of the Pacific by Copernicus
1: number of hurricanes this Atlantic season, which has been exceptionally light due to El Nino, unlike the busy Pacific season
71: death toll in Thailand floods since mid-September
46: orangutans rescued from Indonesia fires by authorities and conservation group YIARI between August and October 9
El Nino is associated with higher global temperatures, and a stronger cycle intensifies the extreme weather patterns it brings to different regions, like drought or heavy rain.
This year's cycle has been called a "super El Nino" but the term many scientists use is "very strong".
The World Meteorological Organization last month said it expected this cycle to meet that definition before it peaks in December.
The benchmark for the definition is the sea-surface temperature anomaly in part of the Pacific Ocean, which is now at record levels.
Climate change complicates the picture because the oceans are now warmer, but scientists can strip out that background effect to determine the absolute rise.

articles.title_orig: AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says
articles.title_zh: AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says
articles.content_orig:
By ALEX BRUMMER CITY EDITOR IN BANGKOK
Updated: 23:15 EDT, 12 October 2026
The global financial system must be on the alert for an AI driven cyberattack that could bring it to a screeching halt, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In a hard-hitting report, the Fund said a serious incident could disrupt critical services including payments systems as well as access to personal bank accounts.
It said finance is a growing source of 'systemic risk' from cyberattack – echoing concerns already publicly expressed by Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey.
Most worryingly, the IMF cautions that AI cyberattacks 'can be hard to contain' and in 70 per cent of recorded cases the software providers concerned had no time to patch up vulnerabilities before hackers exploited them.
The warnings in the Fund's global financial stability report come a day after IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva described AI as 'a slow-moving tsunami' that will wipe out jobs around the world.
IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva
The annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank are taking part in Bangkok in Thailand
At the start of the Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok in Thailand, she said around 40 per cent of all jobs will eventually be 'augmented, downgraded or eliminated' by artificial intelligence.
'It is a slow-moving tsunami but a tsunami nonetheless,' she said.
'It is a transformative technology, it so completely changes how we work, how we live.
'Love it, hate it, or fear it, it is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact.'
But as well as changing the world of work, AI-driven cyberattacks and other hacking incidents pose a major threat to business and the wider financial system.
In Britain, several major retailers including Marks & Spencer and the Co-op and car maker Jaguar Land Rover have suffered severe cyber disruption at a considerable cost to shareholders and anxiety for customers.
Most recently the online fashion retailer ASOS has been caught in the crosshairs of attackers and belatedly let it be known that valuable customer data may have been taken.
A blog by IMF officials argues that 'frontier AI models could accelerate attacks and defences'.
The same report also focuses on the threat an AI correction on the stock market, after rapid rises in the shares of industry pioneers, could trigger a broader slump.
Borrowers – including the UK government and British households with mortgages – have already suffered ructions on the bond market.
The yield on ten-year UK gilts – a key measure of government borrowing costs – has soared to 19-year highs above 5.5 per cent while the 30-year yields have topped 6 per cent for the first time since 1998.
The yield on American treasuries is also on the rise and French bonds are in deep trouble amid speculation that there may have to be a European Central Bank bail-out.
The Fund's experts attribute the rise in yields to renewed inflation fears arising from higher energy prices and over extended government balance sheets. It is noted that yields are at near levels not seen before the financial crisis.
They warn of an 'adverse feedback loop' the combination of fiscal imbalances and the increasing use of debt for speculation in the bond markets. It was such conditions which contributed to Britain's 'Truss tantrum' at the time of the mini budget in October 2022.
Despite the dire warnings the Fund says financial markets have been 'resilient amid solid economic growth' so far. But it added there is no room for 'complacency.'
