articles.title_orig: NY measles spread prompts 'disaster' emergency. It didn't have to be this way, health commissioner says.
articles.title_zh: NY measles spread prompts 'disaster' emergency. It didn't have to be this way, health commissioner says.
articles.content_orig:
Published Oct 12, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. ET
Published Oct 12, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. ET
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Gov. Kathy Hochul has declared a disaster emergency in response to the spread of measles across rural parts of New York state and neighboring Pennsylvania.
But what exactly does that mean?
Dr. James McDonald, the state health commissioner, discussed the disaster declaration and what’s driving it, with All Things Considered host Sean Carlson.
Here’s a transcript of their conversation, edited for length and clarity:
What it means right now is we now have additional authority granted to us by the governor. We have 110 cases of measles so far in New York state. That's more than twice what we had all of last year. The executive order gives us new tools. One tool is, more healthcare workers can administer the vaccine: EMTs, paramedics, pharmacists, community midwives, all trusted people in the community. That helps us.
Another tool we have in the executive order is, we can have more testing done, so nurses can do standing orders and have testing for measles. That helps us find cases quicker, and that will help us identify more cases of measles. The third thing it does is, we get immunization information on adults in our data registry so we know what communities have had the vaccine. That'll help us better plan for where we're likely to see more outbreaks.
It’s rural New York, and really what we're seeing is, there's a lot of local spread in rural New York.
Now, keep in mind, what I mean by that is, it's the most contagious disease out there. So what you see is people come home, and then they spread it to their family, and it spreads really quickly. If your family's not immunized, you're almost all going to get infected. When I say it's the most contagious disease, it doesn't have to be this way. Measles is preventable, almost 100% preventable.
The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — the one that's been around since 1971 — it's the only way to prevent measles, and it really is our best tool in the toolbox. We have to get more people immunized as quickly as possible, so we can really achieve community immunity. We need to get back to that.
One of the things I wanted to underscore nationally is, what's been going on the last two years in the United States is not normal. When you look at the data for 2025, we had almost 2,400 cases of measles in the United States. This year we have almost 3,700 cases and climbing. This is not normal.
What you've been seeing for the prior 25 years was we would average under 100 cases a year, and I don't want us to be desensitized to that. We should not be tolerating thousands of cases as a country every year of a vaccine-preventable disease.
One of the things about measles, it starts out looking like a cough, runny nose, your eyes get watery, maybe a little bit red, and then you get the rash a few days into it, and you might get spots inside your throat. Where it gets really serious is when people get pneumonia. People do end up with respiratory failure. They can end up on breathing machines. About 1 in 5 people we know about with measles are ending up in a hospital.
It is not a mild childhood illness. It is a serious disease. And one of the things that's unusual about the outbreak we're seeing right now is, two out of three cases are in adults.
And one of the things that's important to remember is New York has really good vaccine requirements , but they're school-entry requirements, so if you're an adult between 18 and 69, you really need to have made sure you've had two measles, mumps and rubella vaccines in your life. If you don't know that, contact your local health department or your doctor's office and get a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. It's just that simple.
If you haven't had two measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, you need to be concerned because the vaccine doesn't respect borders. One of the things about measles people need to remember is, people are very contagious four days before they start having symptoms. So they don't even know they're going to have measles, but that's when they're very contagious, and they're contagious four days after their symptoms start, which can be kind of mild.
And this is really the main point: You can't tell that you're being exposed all the time.
Western New York, Central New York, and Northern New York really are the areas I'm most concerned about, and I think it's important to understand that we really don't have great data on adult immunization rates.
The way New York state law is constructed, we know about everyone under 18 who's got an immunization. We don't know about adults. One of the things the executive order gives me, though, is now I'll be able to at least know which adults are getting the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. That will help me. And we have had some success.
You know, it's not always vaccine-hesitant communities. Sometimes there's vaccine-unaware communities. We've administered over 1,200 measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines. What we're finding, though, is after a long conversation, and often it's kitchen-table public health. What I mean by that is local health departments literally going into someone's home, immunizing right at the kitchen table, and if that's where people want to be met, we're all for it. We're happy to meet people where they are, very happy with the way local health departments are literally knocking on doors, offering the vaccine, and answering questions.

articles.title_orig: She broke a Guinness record by accident. Then this St. Louis Park woman doubled down, on purpose.
articles.title_zh: She broke a Guinness record by accident. Then this St. Louis Park woman doubled down, on purpose.
articles.content_orig:
A St. Louis Park, Minnesota, woman broke a Guinness World Record Sunday for rucking a half marathon while carrying a 40 pound pack.
Megan Corey ran the half marathon in two hours and three minutes. The previous record was two hours and 20 minutes. Corey also beat the record for the 20 pound ruck during the same race in Dundas.
"First time going for a Guinness World Record," said Corey. "I found out about the Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon for females carrying a pack when I did a half marathon in Tennessee last year and it was a 20 pound pack half marathon. And found out after from a fellow racer that I had broken the 20 pound record, unbeknownst to me. But you have to predeclare. So today I'm predeclaring and going for the 40 pound record."
The previous 20 pound record was two hours and 34 minutes.

articles.title_orig: GROHE Announces Winner of 2026 GROHE Water Prize at the World Architecture Festival
articles.title_zh: GROHE Announces Winner of 2026 GROHE Water Prize at the World Architecture Festival
articles.content_orig:
The award-winning, "Terracotta Fog Water Harvester" addresses an innovative terracotta facade tile system to harvest atmospheric fog.
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GROHE , a global leader in bathroom solutions and kitchen fittings, has announced the winner of the 2026 GROHE Water Prize for the World Architecture Festival (WAF), slated to be held this year from November 18–20 in Fort Lauderdale.
A Carnegie Mellon University School of Architecture team, spearheaded by Associate Professor and Lead Researcher, Laura Garófalo, has been awarded the £10,000 prize for " Bio-inspired Architectural Terracotta for Sustainable Water Harvesting ," an initiative designed to advance community water self-sufficiency in arid, fog-prone regions. Combining ancient ceramic craftsmanship with digital fabrication and surface physics, the project uses modular terracotta tiles for fog water-harvesting. Drawing design inspiration from leaf venation and the Namib Desert beetle, the tiles pair hydrophilic (water-attracting) clay peaks with hydrophobic (water-repelling) glazed channels to capture fog up to 400% more efficiently than standard flat surfaces.
As a rigid, mineral-based alternative to traditional synthetic plastic netting, the terracotta concept eliminates microplastic pollution while offering a significantly smaller carbon footprint. Designed for future integration into building facades and rainscreen systems, the research shows how exterior walls could one day act as durable, decentralized freshwater collection systems that strengthen local health and climate resilience.
Of the winning project, Patrick Speck, Leader, LIXIL Global Design, Europe & Americas and a jury member of the GROHE Water Prize, remarked: "At GROHE, we believe the future of water stewardship requires rethinking how our built environment interacts with natural resources. By transforming a building facade into an active water-harvesting asset, this project embodies GROHE's design ethos, in which biomimicry, material craft, and human-centered purpose converge to reshape how society experiences water."
"Receiving the Grohe Water Prize is an honor critical to advancing the development of our bio-inspired architectural terracotta system," said Laura Garófolo, Associate Professor at Carnegie Mellon University. "It will make it possible to move through material experimentation toward a scalable architectural application for sustainable water harvesting. We are deeply grateful to GROHE for recognizing the potential of design and architecture to address the growing challenges surrounding water."
Paul Finch, Programme Director, World Architecture Festival, and fellow jury member, added, "As ever, reviewing this year's entries was a pleasure, and we congratulate GROHE for continuing to support this research prize. This year's standout winner offers a brilliant approach to harvesting atmospheric fog - research with clear potential to benefit numerous regions around the world. It is particularly fitting that such an idea should emerge as WAF explores the theme of 'Water' at this year's festival in Fort Lauderdale. We look forward to the project presentation on Thursday, 19 November on the Festival Hall Stage."
With over 50 entries for this year's prize, each submission examined the evolving relationship between water, architecture, and community through innovative, future-focused design. The shortlisted projects demonstrated a remarkable breadth of ideas. Among this year's standout finalists were:
Projecto Vito Volcanic Catchment: An off-grid marine conservation headquarters on Fogo Island featuring vaulted brick roofscapes that serve as the primary rainwater and fog-harvesting system in a region without surface freshwater. Project submitted by Studio Ma (Applicant) with Associação Projecto Vitó — NGO co-applicant (Lead researcher: Christiana Moss, FAIA)
Glasgow Bath Commons: An adaptive reuse project transforming an abandoned railway viaduct and church into a civic water commons that integrates rainwater harvesting, heat recovery, and public bathing culture. Project submitted by Lap Shing Sy.
Lo—TEK Water: A Field Guide for TEKnology: Applied research supporting the Miccosukee–ReefLine Biocultural Stewardship Corridor of Miami Beach, integrating underwater public reef infrastructure with Indigenous co-governance frameworks. Project submitted by Julia Watson
Since 2017, the GROHE Water Prize has supported innovative projects addressing global water challenges, underscoring the transformative potential of water-conscious design for the built environment. While also reflecting the values at the heart of GROHE: combining sustainable innovation, exceptional design, advanced technology, and enduring quality to elevate everyday experiences and help protect one of our planet's most precious resources.
About GROHE GROHE is a leading global brand for complete bathroom solutions and kitchen fittings. Since 2014, GROHE has been a cornerstone of LIXIL's global portfolio of pioneering water and housing brands. To deliver "Pure Freude an Wasser", every product is based on the brand pillars of quality, technology, design and sustainability. From curated experiences within our luxury sub-brand GROHE SPA to refined water solutions for every home, we provide products tailored to the exacting requirements of our professional partners and their differentiated target groups.
With water at the core of everything we do, we manage our value chain and its impact responsibly, contributing to LIXIL's Impact Strategy . By developing technologies that optimize water- and energy-saving potential, we empower a more conscious use of resources without ever compromising on "Pure Freude an Wasser".
About LIXIL LIXIL (TSE Code 5938) makes pioneering water and housing products that solve everyday, real-life challenges, making better homes a reality for everyone, everywhere. Drawing on our Japanese heritage, we create world-leading technology and innovate to make high quality products that transform homes. But the LIXIL difference is how we do this; through meaningful design, an entrepreneurial spirit, a dedication to improving accessibility for all, and responsible business growth. Our approach comes to life through industry leading brands, including INAX, GROHE, American Standard, and TOSTEM. Approximately 53,000 colleagues operating in more than 150 countries are proud to make products that touch the lives of more than a billion people every day. Learn more at www.lixil.com

articles.title_orig: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.title_zh: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
The illustrations are free to use for non-commercial purposes. Attribute ”© Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences”

Robert E. Hall , born 1943 in Palo Alto, CA, USA. PhD 1967 from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA. Professor at Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford , born 1955 in Chicopee, MA, USA. PhD 1983 from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA. Professor at Columbia University, New York, USA.
Prize amount : 12 million Swedish kronor, to be shared equally between the laureates. Further information : www.kva.se and www.nobelprize.org Press contact : Eva Nevelius, Press Secretary, +46 70 878 67 63, [email protected] Experts : Timo Boppart, +41-774 84 30 00, [email protected] , John Hassler, +46 70-811 72 63, [email protected] , Per Krusell, +46 70-276 13 34, [email protected] , members of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, founded in 1739, is an independent organisation whose overall objective is to promote the sciences and strengthen their influence in society. The Academy takes special responsibility for the natural sciences and mathematics, but endeavours to promote the exchange of ideas between various disciplines.

Six prizes were awarded for achievements that have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The 10 laureates' work and discoveries range from optogenetics to efforts to promote peace and international law.

articles.title_orig: How the Cadillac Formula 1® car communicates with engineers around the world in real time
articles.title_zh: How the Cadillac Formula 1® car communicates with engineers around the world in real time
articles.content_orig:
The cars that compete in Formula 1® are unlike any other race cars on earth. They’re like a supercomputer on wheels, gathering massive amounts of data in real time – and sending it to engineers around the world. Those experts use that information to fine-tune the car in pursuit of every last iota of speed and performance.
On the latest episode of GM’s YouTube Series “What Makes Fast,” we get an inside look into exactly how that data is collected, and how it’s shared with engineers around the globe as the car is competing on the track.
The physical side of this is astounding. One expert estimates there could be more than 10 miles of wiring contained inside the Cadillac Formula 1® Team MAC-26 race car, all of it tasked with measuring and communicating the performance of each vehicle component down to the millisecond. Sensors measure the engine’s power output, the tire pressures, even the speed of the air moving around the vehicle as it streaks down the track. The tiniest change in direction is measured, recorded, and broadcast to experts at the track and between the engineering headquarters in Silverstone, England and Charlotte, North Carolina.
This data doesn’t just tell the racing engineers how the car is performing in the moment. It also guides them as they decide to make adjustments to the car – either in real-time during the race, or in preparation for the next competition. That data is also fed into the highly-accurate GM “Driver In Loop” simulator in Charlotte that the team uses to practice and prepare for the next race.
It’s a high-pressure job. “It’s definitely a weight on our shoulders,” says Ryan Tincher, IT Operations Manager at GM Motorsports. “But it’s not anything the team shies away from… it’s part of what brings everybody back every weekend.”

articles.title_orig: Why IonQ Is Betting Big on Quantum Cybersecurity With $1.3 Billion Elisity Acquisition
articles.title_zh: Why IonQ Is Betting Big on Quantum Cybersecurity With $1.3 Billion Elisity Acquisition
articles.content_orig:
College Park, Md. - Oct. 12, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion. The acquisition brings together IonQ's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities with Elisity's enterprise Zero Trust technology platform. On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.
Elisity builds on IonQ’s expanding quantum security offerings with a high-growth enterprise security business, cutting-edge Zero Trust technology platform, and team of industry leaders led by cybersecurity expert CEO James Winebrenner. Elisity has a strong track record of doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year with zero churn among deployed customers. With more than 100 global customer deployments and deep CISO and security community relationships, Elisity will provide IonQ with expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation opportunity with double-digit CAGR to IonQ.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.”
Elisity’s Commercial Advantage
Enterprises face two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that operate at machine speed and preparing to protect sensitive information against future quantum threats. The urgency of this transition is underscored by recent White House executive orders advancing quantum innovation and accelerating the federal government's migration to PQC. These directives reinforce the importance of securing critical systems and preparing government networks for quantum-era threats while supporting long-term modernization.
Today, Elisity IdentityGraph combines native asset identity and partner-enriched context, and risk information to inform least-privilege access policy for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. Teams can simulate policies before limiting each identity to the communications it needs, helping reduce attack surface and contain an attack’s spread. By bringing together Elisity's Zero Trust framework with IonQ's PQC and QKD capabilities, the companies will combine cryptographic protection for sensitive information and communications with identity-based controls that limit unauthorized access and the spread of threats across enterprise networks. The shared roadmap with IonQ will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information. This integrated approach will help customers address quantum-related security risks through a multiyear transition while strengthening defenses against current cyberattacks, including threats involving AI agents.
Following closing, Elisity will continue serving its customers under its current leadership, including current CEO James Winebrenner. Together, the companies will continue their track record of innovation, customer success and strong partner relationships, backed by IonQ’s demonstrated approach of investing in the critical technologies it acquires.
IonQ’s Multiproduct Revenue Growth Opportunity
IonQ brings an established track record in growing its quantum security and quantum-secure communications offering. The company has deployed some of the largest quantum-safe national communications networks in the world, including in Switzerland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and serves global customers with quantum-safe defense in depth spanning quantum-safe posture management, quantum key distribution, and post quantum cryptography.
Customers are increasingly adopting multiple IonQ products and services, driving growth in multiproduct revenue and providing evidence of demand for integrated solutions; in the second quarter of 2026, IonQ delivered 40% year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue..
IonQ and Elisity expect opportunities to cross-sell complementary security solutions, expand relationships with enterprise and government customers, and develop integrated offerings.
Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business. The number of IonQ shares to be issued in the transaction will be calculated at closing based on the volume weighted average price of IonQ common stock for the 20 trading days prior to, but not including, the third business day before the closing date, but that price will not be greater than $49.61 or less than $33.07 per share.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Elisity helps enterprises advance Zero Trust security for users, devices, workloads, AI agents and other non-human identities. Elisity IdentityGraph correlates identity, asset and risk information from native and partner sources to inform access decisions. Elisity’s software policy layer uses the network to enforce access rules independently of the underlying network technology. Teams can simulate policies and limit each identity to the communications it needs, extending the value of existing network and security investments. Founded in 2019, Elisity has a global employee footprint and a growing number of customers in the Fortune 500. Learn more at elisity.com .
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: NATO general sets out tough military response to any 'foolish' Russian attack
articles.title_zh: NATO general sets out tough military response to any 'foolish' Russian attack
articles.content_orig:
Professor Azeem Ibrahim says Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic enclave has become a testing ground for hybrid warfare targeting European infrastructure.
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that what he called the "lethal alliance" would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault.
"Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland , in an apparent warning to Moscow.
"This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force," he said during a panel titled "Theory of Victory: How Do We Achieve Military Success Against Russia in Deterrence and Defence?" on the first day of the forum.
US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that the alliance would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe, also outlined a three-pronged strategy of "blocking, blunting and breaking" enemy forces, making clear that while NATO is a defensive alliance, it is prepared to respond decisively to an assault on any of its 32 members.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile."
The warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow.
"We stand here together in Poland today stronger than ever united in our common vision of a more balanced, more ready and more lethal alliance," Grynkewich also said.
European officials have accused Russia of waging a campaign of hybrid warfare involving sabotage, arson and cyberattacks, alongside increasingly provocative military activity near NATO territory.
I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA
Grynkewich's warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
In 2025, multiple Russian drones entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on Ukraine, prompting a response from Polish and allied aircraft.
NATO launched Operation Eastern Sentry to strengthen defenses along its eastern flank.
Romania has also reported Russian drone incursions , while Estonia has accused Russian military aircraft of violating its airspace.
Grynkewich's remarks had followed a tense weekend between Russia and Ukraine, with Moscow launching fresh strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite diplomatic efforts to reduce hostilities.
President Donald Trump had announced that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the U.S. and global markets.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania. ( Photo by Contributor/Getty Images)
The reported agreement included a waiver of certain U.S. sanctions on Russian energy exports.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, casting doubt on prospects for a broader ceasefire.
The tensions have also been accompanied by recent nuclear warnings from Moscow.
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad , its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic note obtained by Reuters , Moscow accused NATO of pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" that carried "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
According to the note, Russia warned it could use its full military arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend Kaliningrad and raised the possibility of strikes against decision-making centers in NATO countries at the outset of a conflict.
RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE
The Hague, Netherlands - In photos, NATO leaders participate in the summit in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 25, 2025. NATO countries pledged to increase their defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, as demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump. The summit's final declaration states that countries will invest "at least 3.5%" of their GDP annually in military capabilities and an additional 1.5% in protecting critical infrastructure. (Handout / Latin America News Agency via Reuters Connect)
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte rejected the threats, emphasizing the alliance's defensive mission and calling on Moscow to end its war in Ukraine.
"Putin knows that he can never win from NATO," Rutte said during a Sept. 30 appearance at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit .
Putin has also maintained that Russia has no plans to attack European countries and wants peaceful coexistence with its neighbors.
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name during his Warsaw address, but his warning appeared directed at Moscow and with NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept also identifying Russia as the most significant and direct threat to allied security.
"My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance," Grynkewich said on Monday.
"And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us."
Grynkewich said NATO was already putting the strategy into action through military exercises, enhanced military readiness and investments in new capabilities.
SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS
NATO Secretary Gen. Mark Rutte attempts to assure President Donald Trump on Wednesday in a news conference that allies are increasing their financial commitments so Europe's defense is not all on the U.S. taxpayers. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
"If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent," he said.
The general made clear that NATO's response would not necessarily be limited to enemy troops directly involved in an assault, but could extend to the broader military infrastructure enabling the attack.
Meanwhile, Trump has pressed European allies to increase defense spending and has questioned whether countries that fail to meet their obligations should expect U.S. protection.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment, recalling Trump's positive remarks about the alliance during the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands.
"I was in the room and I felt the love," Grynkewich said of the 2025 event.
"What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we've got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he added.
He also indicated a willingness to discuss suspected hybrid attacks more openly if individual NATO governments wanted him to address their concerns.
"If a nation wants me to, I'm happy to talk about it," he said.

articles.title_orig: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.title_zh: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction in Southeast: "Never expected to be 77 years old and go through this"
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction in Southeast: "Never expected to be 77 years old and go through this"
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias left behind a trail of destruction from Florida's Gulf Coast to the Carolinas over the weekend after slamming onto shore near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm.
The storm made landfall on Friday night and roared through the Southeast. At least two people were killed in Florida and two were killed in Alabama.
Some of the most violent wind gusts from the hurricane were recorded 15 miles away from the coast, in Milton, Florida. The wind there took down a massive tree, which fell on top of a house. Phyllis Hennebery said she was in her room lying down when the tree fell.
"I never expected to be 77 years old and go through this," she said, showing CBS News destruction from the fallen tree in the ceiling above her.
The hurricane shredded roofs off apartments and tore away walls that once enclosed bedrooms. On Monday morning, more than 150,000 customers in Florida were still without power, according to poweroutage.us . More than 20,000 others were without power in Alabama.
Pastor Jonathan Kaushal's church group was handing out food and water after the storm.
"Lots of people in need after the hurricane and so we just want to be there for the community," he said.
The remnants of the storm also spun off at least eight confirmed tornadoes in Georgia and the Carolinas, including one that ripped off the roof of a home about 90 miles west of Charleston.
In western North Carolina, more than half a foot of rain flooded roads.
As Isaias moved through the Southeast, the West Coast was feeling the impact of another significant storm. What's left of Tropical Storm Rachel sent massive 8-foot waves pounding beachfront homes south of Los Angeles.
The Coast Guard rescued a man by helicopter who was trapped in a sailboat that ran onshore Sunday morning.
Flooding also spread into southern Nevada, swamping the Las Vegas Strip.
Severe weather also slammed Utah during the Moab 240, a five-day-long ultramarathon. Around 70 runners were rescued by bus after they were stranded by dangerous floods.

articles.title_orig: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.title_zh: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.content_orig:
(OSV News) — Prominent political and religious leaders from around the world expressed well wishes and prayers for Pope Leo XIV after he announced he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule.
The pope made the surprise announcement while addressing pilgrims Oct. 11 during his Sunday Angelus address.
After doctors detected “a small, localized nodule” in his lung, Pope Leo said he would follow their advice and “undergo surgery to remove it.”
“The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days,” he said. ” I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers.”
Not long after his announcement, Italian President Sergio Mattarella published a letter to Pope Leo saying that the news of his surgery “was received with deep empathy and emotion by all the Italian people.”
“In view of your hospitalization in the coming days, may the affectionate thoughts of all Italians reach you, which I convey while adding my own personal sentiments,” Mattarella wrote. “The Italian people stand close to you.”
The Italian head of state said the pope could count on the prayers of not only the Catholic faithful, but also “on the caring thoughts of countless people, in Italy as well as across the world, whether believers or non-believers.”
Several world leaders also took to X to send well wishes to the pope, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who wished Pope Leo “a successful surgery and a swift, full recovery.”
“Our thoughts and prayers are with him, and we hope he will soon be back in good health and strength,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Ukraine is deeply grateful to His Holiness for his prayers and his strong, consistent calls for a dignified and durable peace.”
In a brief message posted to X, Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrote: “From the holy city of Jerusalem, I wish Pope Leo XIV a full and speedy recovery.”
Maltese Prime Minister Robert Abela also extended “prayers and best wishes” to the pope for “a successful procedure and a complete recovery.”
Pope Leo also received prayers from Anglican Archbishop Sarah Mullaly of Canterbury, who said she was “holding Pope Leo XIV in my prayers over these coming days, asking for God’s protection, closeness and care.”
“With Christians across the country and around the world, I pray for the pope’s swift recovery,” the head of the Church of England wrote on X.
Viktor Eichner, the World Jewish Congress’ representative to the Holy See, also posted on X, writing: “On behalf of the World Jewish Congress, I wish Pope Leo XIV a successful surgery and a speedy recovery. May he return to full strength soon.”
The surgery announcement came as Pope Leo prepares to embark on his longest international trip to date: a 12-day apostolic visit to Latin America, including stops in Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.
At the Angelus, the pope greeted a group of Peruvian pilgrims and thanked them for praying for his upcoming visit, indicating the trip was still moving forward.
At a press conference in Uruguay, the first stop in the pope’s Nov. 6-17 apostolic trip, Cardinal Daniel Sturla of Montevideo told journalists Oct. 11 that although the announcement “was a surprise,” the pope’s greetings to the Peruvian pilgrims showed that “the plans remain the same.”
“Obviously, we are all praying for the pope’s health and trust that everything will go well, that he will recover and be able to be here on the scheduled date,” Cardinal Sturla said.
When asked if any precautions will be taken given that the pope is expected to arrive in less than a month, the Uruguayan cardinal said he believed so and that the pope “always travels accompanied by his personal physician and other healthcare staff.”
“I understand that some care will need to be taken,” Cardinal Sturla said. “We will be instructed in the coming days. We will be very attentive to that, but confident that everything will go well and that we are moving forward.”
Argentine President Javier Milei extended his “affection and best wishes” ahead of the pope’s surgery. Pope Leo will visit Argentina Nov. 8-11.
“All of Argentina accompanies His Holiness with affection and prayer, wishing him a prompt and full recovery,” Milei wrote on X. “From our country, we join in prayer for his health, in the hope that he may soon continue guiding the Church with his characteristic wisdom and strength.”
The Argentine bishops’ conference issued a statement calling on the country’s Catholics to pray for Pope Leo ahead of his surgery.
“We ask the Lord to grant him strength and peace at this time, that the surgery proceeds favorably, and that he may achieve a prompt and full recovery,” the bishops wrote.
Noting the pope’s “serenity and confidence” in his announcement, the bishops urged Catholics to “remain spiritually united with him.”
In Peru, where Pope Leo is scheduled to visit Nov. 11-17, President Keiko Fujimori took to X to express her and her country’s “profound affection and solidarity” with the pope “in the face of this health issue, which we hope he will overcome fully and successfully.”
“Our hearts and our prayers are with him, in the hope of soon having him among us,” Fujimori wrote. “With deep faith and hope, we pray that the Holy Father has a prompt recovery and may continue guiding, with wisdom and strength, the path of faith of the entire Holy Church.”
In a statement released shortly after the pope’s announcement, Bishop Carlos Enrique García Camader of Lurin, president of the Peruvian bishops’ conference, noted the pope’s “profound serenity and transparency” in announcing his surgery and that his “testimony of fortitude and humility in sharing this news moves us and immediately calls us to unity in prayer.”
“The Peruvian Episcopate invites all Catholic people and people of goodwill to unite in prayer for the health of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, raising our supplications to God, Lord of life and source of all health, so that He may strengthen him and grant him the health required for the fulfillment of his mission,” Bishop García wrote.
He also invoked Mary’s intercession “so that in the fullness of his strength he may continue fulfilling his mission in service to the Church and all humanity, continuing to be a messenger of peace and hope, and a witness of unity, fraternity, and encounter among all peoples.”
Junno Arocho Esteves is an international correspondent for OSV News. Follow him on X @jae_journalist

articles.title_orig: At least 20 injured in northern Israel explosion
articles.title_zh: At least 20 injured in northern Israel explosion
articles.content_orig:
One person has been killed and 19 others were injured in an explosion in northern Israel near the Lebanese border, according to preliminary official tallies, in an incident that is under investigation.
“I share in the heavy grief of the family of the boy who was killed in the explosion during the trip near the northern border, and I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured,” Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz posted on X, adding that authorities were looking into the cause of the blast.
Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the victim was a 15-year-old who had gone on an annual school trip.
Citing medical sources, the Israeli police earlier said that “the initial suspicion is that it was caused by an unexploded ordnance, as a result of which about 20 people were injured with varying degrees of severity.” The explosion occurred near the community of Neot Mordechai, between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftach.
The incident injured both students and staff from a religious high school as they were on an outing, the municipality of the northern city of Maalot-Tarshiha said.
There is a heavy military deployment in the north of the country and in parts of southern Lebanon as Israel continues attacks it says target the Iran-aligned Hezbollah group.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said that some of the injured are described to be in critical condition.
“There is very little specific information as to what happened, what the source of that explosion was, but it’s certainly a reminder that Northern Israel, the upper Galilee and particularly the border with Lebanon remains an area where there is a military operation, with the Israeli military deployed and where thousands of munitions were used over the past 3 years”, Odeh said.
Odeh said the explosion had “mobilised” Israel’s political echelons, with the Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu heading to the area, and the Israeli minister of National Security National Ben Gvir canceling a political engagement that was on his agenda.
Tens of thousands of Israelis living in the country’s north were forced to leave the region after Lebanon’s Hezbollah group started firing rockets following Israel’s genocidal 2023 war in Gaza.
In March, Israeli forces started occupying southern Lebanon following a renewal of hostilities after the US – Israel war on Iran. The military said soldiers and helicopters had been dispatched to the scene in northern Israel, a region from which Israeli forces have been pounding Lebanon, whose Hezbollah militants have fired periodic rockets across the border.
Odeh says most residents have not returned because they “did not have the confidence” that the government will be able to protect them.
“They saw the extensive damage that rockets were exacting on their communities and many them, according reports, have not been encouraged to return because the situation remains volatile”, she said.

articles.title_orig: The OnePlus 16 is the company’s most interesting phone in years
articles.title_zh: The OnePlus 16 is the company’s most interesting phone in years
articles.content_orig:
But it’s not launching in the US or Europe.
But it’s not launching in the US or Europe.
Today the OnePlus 16 launched in China, the company’s first flagship phone since quitting both the US and European markets this summer. As luck would have it, it also looks like the company’s best phone in some time.
Like most OnePlus phones, the 16 is positioned around performance, with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset , and up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. That’s backed up by an enormous 9,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, one of the biggest seen in any Android flagship yet. 100W wired and 50W wireless charging complete the power setup.
On the display front, the phone jumps to a 185Hz OLED panel for the first time. That’ll not only be used for 185fps gaming in compatible titles, but can also run at up to 165Hz throughout the system UI — a first for high refresh rate panels like this.
Even the cameras, not usually OnePlus’ strong suit, have had a meaningful upgrade. The main camera has a higher resolution (200 megapixels), larger sensor (1/1.4-inch-type), and faster aperture (f/1.4) than the OnePlus 15’s. That should help, given we found that phone’s camera had frustrating “imitations in low light.” 50-megapixel ultrawide and telephoto cameras round out the rear trio, and the latter also enjoys a big bump to a 1/1.95-inch sensor.
There’s a design flourish too, with the phone’s silver finish including LED lighting that features a big “16” and what the company claims is a set of galactic coordinates. While the shapes of the lights are fixed, they’ll reportedly flash with different rhythms to notify you of calls, messages, battery level, and more.
The OnePlus 16 is available in China starting from ¥5,699 (about $850). With OnePlus no longer in either the US or Europe, there’s no hope of a launch for the 16 in either market.

articles.title_orig: Are banks, the USPS and stock market open on Columbus Day? Here is what to know.
articles.title_zh: Are banks, the USPS and stock market open on Columbus Day? Here is what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Columbus Day, also known as Indigenous Peoples Day, may be an official federal holiday, but it's not consistently observed across the U.S., according to the Pew Research Center.
Falling on the second Monday in October, the holiday creates a three-day weekend for workers whose employers observe it, including federal employees and some state workers, Pew found.
But a push to shift recognition away from explorer Christopher Columbus and instead honor North America's original inhabitants means the holiday isn't as widely observed as it once was.
Since Oct. 12 is a federal holiday, some services and businesses will be closed. Here's what to know about what is open and closed on Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples Day.
Yes, Monday, Oct. 12, is a federal holiday, which means that U.S. government offices will be closed and federal workers have the day off.
Yes, the stock market is open on Columbus Day, with neither the New York Stock Exchange nor the Nasdaq market observing it as a holiday.
The stock market will be open during its regular working hours on Monday from 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. ET.
No, the U.S. Postal Service observes Columbus Day as a holiday, which means there will be no regular residential or business mail delivery. All USPS offices will also be closed.
It's best to check with your bank, as some are open while others observe the holiday.
JPMorgan Chase said that its branches will be open on Oct. 12, but will treat the day as a holiday for online transactions. That means customers can't schedule transactions to occur on Columbus Day, and repeating transactions were processed on the preceding business day.
Many other banks are closed on Columbus Day, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America .
Yes, Costco is open for business today, as Columbus Day isn't among the seven holidays the discount chain observes.
Walmart is also open on Columbus Day, with stores open during regular hours, according to the retailer's website.

articles.title_zh: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background
articles.content_orig:

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context.
There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns.
Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time.
The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin.
Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting note-takers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day.
Meeting note-taking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself.
The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another.
“The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” the company’s co-founder and CEO, Mo, told TechCrunch.
The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar.
The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information.
Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third-parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech.
Some meeting note-takers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversation and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Voice Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns .
Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem.
“We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said.
Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech recognition models.

articles.title_orig: US Homeland Security defends Nidal Hasan livestream execution bid
articles.title_zh: US Homeland Security defends Nidal Hasan livestream execution bid
articles.content_orig:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief has defended a plan to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan, rejecting claims that it could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr.
"I don't see an elevated risk," Markwayne Mullin said on Sunday. "I think people need to understand that if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime."
Hasan, a former US Army Major, is due to be executed by firing squad in December for shooting dead 13 soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Trump administration has said it plans to livestream his death, prompting shock and concern from both Republicans and Democrats.
President Donald Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.
It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week , has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.
Alaskan Republican Senator, Lisa Murkowski, called the decision "gruesome" and said livestreaming an execution was something she would expect "from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America".
"It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks," she wrote on X , adding that "how we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself."
Virginia Democrat Mark Warner said that allowing the public to tune into the execution could heighten the national security risk.
"Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk," he wrote .
But speaking to CBS news programme Face the Nation on Sunday, the DHS secretary rejected these concerns, and insisted the risks had been considered.
"[Hasan] killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies," Mullin told presenter Margaret Brennan.
Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed troops at a crowded medical building at the Fort Hood military base. A further 32 others were injured in the attack.
In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes" and said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.
His execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the military's first execution by firing squad since World War Two.

From Gallup to Singapore, Adam Becenti has found cultural connection, spiritual strength and community through competitive paddling
Adam Becenti, a Diné paddler from Gallup, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples Day by honoring his roots and showcasing his abilities on the global stage.
Becenti grew up playing sports commonly offered in the New Mexico desert while also participating in Diné ceremonies and learning about his culture from his father.
After moving to Portland, Oregon, in 2013, he joined a Native dragon boat team made up of Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission employees. He began outrigger canoeing in 2017, eventually finding that paddling offered more than exercise and competition.
For Becenti, the sport provides mental, physical, emotional and spiritual benefits while connecting him with Indigenous paddling traditions around the world.
"As a Diné person, we hold water sacred," Becenti said. "Every time I get on the water, I try to make an offering and ultimately connect in those ways."
Paddling has taken Becenti to Japan and New Zealand, where he has learned from other cultures and built relationships with Indigenous communities. He said those experiences showed him that paddling is more than a sport; it is a culture, lifestyle and generational tradition for many Indigenous peoples.
In August, Becenti represented the United States and the Pacific Northwest at the 2026 World Sprints. His team reached the semifinals in its strongest races.
Although the team did not advance as far as it had hoped, Becenti said competing alongside some of the world’s top paddlers and participating in cultural exchanges felt like a victory.
Now living in Seattle, Becenti paddles on Lake Washington and plans to train for distance championships and attempt to qualify for future sprint championships.
His advice to others is to travel, embrace new experiences and build relationships with people from different cultures without forgetting who they are or where they come from.

articles.title_orig: Real-World Nonhormonal Therapy Effects on VMS Bother, Work, and Mood
articles.title_zh: Real-World Nonhormonal Therapy Effects on VMS Bother, Work, and Mood
articles.content_orig:
Pauline M. Maki, PhD, reviews early OPTION-VMS findings showing improvements in hot flash bother, work productivity, depression, and anxiety with fezolinetant (Veozah).
This content is sponsored by Astellas, Inc but was independently developed by MJH Life Sciences
Pauline M. Maki, PhD, reviews the first data cuts from OPTION-VMS, released at The Menopause Society 2025 meeting. These analyses examined bother from VMS, meaning hot flashes and night sweats, using the MENQOL, a commonly used measure of vasomotor symptom (VMS) bother, along with a widely used measure of workplace productivity. 1
She describes the results as very reassuring because they replicated what was seen in the trials. Where the SKYLIGHT trials showed benefits of fezolinetant (Veozah) on VMS frequency and severity, the original OPTION-VMS data cut showed improvement in women's reported bother from hot flashes. The primary time point was 12 weeks, Maki notes, but improvement was also observed at 4 and 8 weeks, indicating early benefit. In what she calls a critically important outcome, women also reported a substantial boost within 12 weeks in workplace productivity and in activity levels outside of work. This suggests, she explains, that relief from hot flashes and hot flash bother translates to real-world improvement in women's ability to function in daily life.
Maki then turns to new outcome data presented at the Endocrine Society meeting in 2026 on the effects of fezolinetant and other nonhormonal interventions for VMS on depression and anxiety. The study used the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, widely used measures that many providers already have access to in their clinics. Because participants presented to clinics seeking care for VMS, Maki explains, most did not have substantial depression or anxiety at baseline, and levels at the first study visit were minimal. Even with this minimal burden, depression and anxiety improved with fezolinetant after 12 weeks. 2 As a researcher in women's mental health, she finds this especially interesting, and says it suggests secondary benefits for women whose bothersome menopause symptoms are effectively treated.
In the next segment, Maki explains how wrist-worn actigraphy captures sleep problems women underreport and what it shows with fezolinetant vs SSRIs and SNRIs.

articles.title_orig: Mato’s AI Talent Interviews Humans
articles.title_zh: Mato’s AI Talent Interviews Humans
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
Mato is a media platform that uses AI to help companies turn their expertise into professionally produced podcasts and media.
“We’re building the first generation of AI talents that interview real humans, creating authentic content at a scale that was never before possible,” it states.
Mato has been awarded an ElevenLabs grant, received AWS Activate credits and is a member of NVIDIA Inception.
Alexander Benz is co-founder and CEO.
Radio World: What is Mato?
Alexander Benz: Mato is a Los Angeles-based media technology company founded in 2024 by my husband, Edward Benz, and me. The company is privately held, and we recently raised a pre-seed investment from Mucker Capital and joined MuckerLab .
Mato gives companies AI agents that interview real human guests live. The AI host prepares for the subject, conducts an unscripted interview, listens to what the guest actually says, and asks followup questions in real time. The conversation can then move through editing, transcripts, clips, cover art and distribution, with the customer retaining final approval.
RW: Tell us more about it and how it might be used by radio broadcasters or related audio fields.
Benz: The core product is the live AI interviewer.
Most AI audio tools start with text and generate something from it. Mato starts with a person. A real guest joins an interview, speaks naturally, and the AI host conducts the conversation in real time.
A public demonstration of the AI interviewer is available , which includes a Kevin DeMeritt interview, transcript and follow-up timestamps.
For radio, I think the interesting part is what that does to the economics and logistics of producing expert-led audio. A broadcaster can capture interviews, recurring expert segments, branded programming or niche shows without needing a human host and full production team around every recording session.
Since we first spoke, we’ve brought this into traditional radio with Lear Capital. Their Mato-produced show “ Outside the Dollar ” uses AI-hosted interviews with real guests and is now being distributed for radio as well as digital listening.
RW: What prompted the development of a tool that uses an AI host to conduct interviews?
Benz: We were much more interested in whether AI could conduct a good conversation than whether it could generate another piece of content.
There is an enormous amount of useful knowledge sitting inside companies with founders, customers, executives and subject-matter experts. Traditional podcast production makes capturing that knowledge relatively expensive and operationally heavy.
The question became: What happens if the AI does the preparation, interviewing and much of the production work, while the expertise still comes from an actual person?
RW: How do your guardrails assure that the final interview is correct and appropriate?
Benz: We do not claim that an AI interviewer can guarantee that every statement a guest makes is factually correct.
Our approach is to preserve provenance and human editorial control instead.
The recorded human conversation remains the source. Customers can set the subject, questions and editorial boundaries before an interview, and they retain final approval before anything is released. The transcript and recording also make it possible to review the finished material against what the guest actually said.
The AI is responsible for conducting and processing the conversation. It does not become the authority on the subject being discussed.
RW: What is the experience of being interviewed by an AI host like?
Benz: It feels much closer to being interviewed by a person than completing a questionnaire or talking to a traditional chatbot.
The guest joins, the AI host asks a question, and the guest answers naturally. While they are speaking, the agent is listening to the substance of the answer and deciding what makes sense to ask next.
So if someone introduces an unexpected detail, the host can follow that thread rather than simply moving to question number three on a predetermined list.
The guest does not need to write prompts or learn how to use an AI tool. Their job is simply to talk about what they know.
RW: How can an interested reader learn more or hear an example?
Benz: Lear Capital’s “Outside the Dollar” is a useful current example because it shows the model in an actual subject-matter interview rather than a scripted demonstration.
We also have several public interviews and product examples available through Mato, along with a press kit containing screenshots and company information.
RW: What else should we know?
Benz: The distinction that matters most to us is that we are not trying to synthesize the human out of media.
There are already plenty of AI products that can generate an article, a voice or a podcast from a prompt. Mato is built around the opposite premise: The interesting material should still come from a real person.
We want AI to remove much of the coordination and production work required to capture that person’s knowledge, rather than replacing the person whose knowledge made the content worth producing in the first place.
Podcasting is our first use case, but we see the broader product as a conversation layer for capturing human knowledge.

articles.title_orig: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.title_zh: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.content_orig:
In a new video for the centennial, Pope Leo reflects on his personal connection to World Mission Sunday, from his childhood in the United States to his years of missionary service in Peru.
Ahead of the 100th World Mission Sunday on the weekend of October 17-18, Pope Leo XIV released a personal video message reflecting on the extraordinary day.
100 years ago, when World Mission Sunday began, there were about 9.6 million Catholics living in 296 mission jurisdictions. Today, that number has grown to more than 346 million Catholics living in 1,131 mission territories.
These individuals are served through more than 41,000 parishes, 124,309 Catholic schools and 26, 318 social institutions.
When he was a child, Pope Leo XIV celebrated World Mission Sunday in the United States. Later, when he was a priest and bishop in Peru, he was the recipient of the generous prayers and support of Catholics around the world.
Now, as pope, he celebrates the centennial of the mission-supporting international collection and expresses gratitude for the Church's loving support of our brothers and sisters worldwide.
To support World Mission Sunday, Catholics across Northern Colorado may donate to their parish with "World Mission Sunday" in the memo line of their donation. For more information, visit the Pontifical Mission Societies' website here .
